Complaint Against Mortgage Lender Regarding Misleading Promotion and Failure to Disclose Material Terms I am submitting this complaint regarding a promotional offer advertised by my mortgage lender, which stated that if they could not meet or beat a competitors loan offer, they would provide a gift card equal to my first principal and interest payment, up to {$2000.00}. 

During my interaction with the companys representative, I explicitly referenced this promotion and asked about it directly. I also clearly explained that I had received a significantly lower rate offer ( approximately 4 % ) from another lender and asked if they could match or beat it. 

The representative acknowledged my inquiry and responded by asking me to send the competing offer so they could review it and see what they could do. At no point during this conversation did the representative disclose any limitations, exclusions, or conditions associated with the promotion. 

Importantly, I made it clear that the competing offer involved Servicemembers Civil Relief Act ( SCRA ) benefits and was associated with another lender. I later provided documentation supporting this, including proof that clearly identified the competing lender, which is a credit union. 

Despite having this information, the representative never informed me that credit union offers would be excluded from the promotion, nor did they indicate that my documentation would not qualify. Instead, I was repeatedly told that the documentation I provided was not sufficient, without any clear explanation of what specific requirement was not being met. 

After the fact, the company is now asserting that I do not qualify for the promotion due to terms and conditions that were never disclosed to me during my interaction with their representative. They have also stated that they never directly offered the promotion to me. 

However, this response confirms that my understanding of the promotion came entirely from their representative, and that I was not provided with the official terms or conditions at the time of my inquiry. As a result, I reasonably relied on the information provided during our direct communication. 

If the promotion contained material limitationssuch as exclusions related to credit unions or specific documentation requirementsthose terms should have been clearly and explicitly disclosed at the time I inquired about the promotion, especially after I provided details about the competing offer. 

By failing to disclose these key eligibility requirements while actively engaging with me about the promotion and encouraging me to submit documentation, the company created a misleading impression that the promotion applied to my situation. 

I have also provided screenshots of my communications with the companys representative, which demonstrate that : I explicitly referenced the promotion I disclosed the nature of the competing offer The representative encouraged me to submit documentation No exclusions or disqualifying conditions were communicated I believe this constitutes a failure to properly disclose material terms and conditions, and a misleading representation of a promotional offer. 

Desired Resolution : I am requesting that the company honor the promotional offer as it was presented to me during my interaction, or otherwise provide an appropriate resolution consistent with the advertised terms.

XX/XX/XXXX, XXXXWells Fargo sent a letter requesting additional information by XX/XX/XXXX. 

After receiving this letter, I contacted Wells Fargo 's Claims Assistance Center. During that conversation, the representative changed the reason associated with my claim.

Why the basis for denial continued to change.

Why Wells Fargo initially concluded that the merchant needed additional time. 
Why Wells Fargo later changed its conclusion. 
What evidence supported any of its determinations.

Except as otherwise provided in this section, a consumer reporting agency shall block the reporting of any information in the file of a consumer that the consumer identifies as information that resulted from an alleged identity theft, not later than 4 business days after the date of receipt by such agency of ( 1 ) appropriate proof of the identity of the consumer ; ( 2 ) a copy of an identity theft report ; ( 3 ) the identification of such information by the consumer; and ( 4 ) a statement by the consumer that the information is not information relating to any transaction by the consumer. ( b ) Notification. A consumer reporting agency shall promptly notify the furnisher of information identified by the consumer under subsection ( a ) of this section ( 1 ) that the information may be a result of identity theft ; ( 2 ) that an identity theft report has been filed ; ( 3 ) that a block has been requested under this section; and ( 4 ) of the effective dates of the block. ( c ) Authority to decline or rescind. ( 1 ) In general. A consumer reporting agency may decline to block, or may rescind any block, of information relating to a consumer under this section, if the consumer reporting agency reasonably determines that ( A ) the information was blocked in error or a block was requested by the consumer in error ; ( B ) the information was blocked, or a block was requested by the consumer, on the basis of a material misrepresentation of fact by the consumer relevant to the request to block ; or ( C ) the consumer obtained possession of goods, services, or money as a result of the blocked transaction or transactions. ( 2 ) Notification to consumer. If a block of information is declined or rescinded under this subsection, the affected consumer shall be notified promptly, in the same manner as consumers are notified of the reinsertion of information under section 1681i ( a ) ( 5 ) ( B ) of this title. ( 3 ) Significance of block. For purposes of this subsection, if a consumer reporting agency rescinds a block, the presence of information in the file of a consumer prior to the blocking of such information is not evidence of whether the consumer knew or should have known that the consumer obtained possession of any goods, services, or money as a result of the block. ( d ) Exception for resellers. ( 1 ) No reseller file. This section shall not apply to a consumer reporting agency, if the consumer reporting agency ( A ) is a reseller ; ( B ) is not, at the time of the request of the consumer under subsection ( a ) of this section, otherwise furnishing or reselling a consumer report concerning the information identified by the consumer ; and ( C ) informs the consumer, by any means, that the consumer may report the identity theft to the Bureau to obtain consumer information regarding identity theft. ( 2 ) Reseller with file. The sole obligation of the consumer reporting agency under this section, with regard to any request of a consumer under this section, shall be to block the consumer report maintained by the consumer reporting agency from any subsequent use, if ( A ) the consumer, in accordance with the provisions of subsection ( a ) of this section, identifies, to a consumer reporting agency, information in the file of the consumer that resulted from identity theft ; and ( B ) the consumer reporting agency is a reseller of the identified information. ( 3 ) Notice. In carrying out its obligation under paragraph ( 2 ), the reseller shall promptly provide a notice to the consumer of the decision to block the file. Such notice shall contain the name, address, and telephone number of each consumer reporting agency from which the consumer information was obtained for resale. ( e ) Exception for verification companies. The provisions of this section do not apply to a check services company, acting as such, which issues authorizations for the purpose of approving or processing negotiable instruments, electronic fund transfers, or similar methods of payments, except that, beginning 4 business days after receipt of information described in paragraphs ( 1 ) through ( 3 ) of subsection ( a ) of this section, a check services company shall not report to a national consumer reporting agency described in section 1681a ( p ) of this title, any information identified in the subject identity theft report as resulting from identity theft. ( f ) Access to blocked information by law enforcement agencies. No provision of this section shall be construed as requiring a consumer reporting agency to prevent a Federal, State, or local law enforcement agency from accessing blocked information in a consumer file to which the agency could otherwise obtain access under this subchapter.

I am disputing the accuracy of a deficiency balance Hyundai Capital America is reporting on my credit file in the amount of approximately {$26000.00}, arising from a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX XXXX ) financed through Hyundai Capital America. 
The vehicle was financed in XX/XX/XXXX. I stopped making payments in early XXXX. In approximately XX/XX/XXXX, the vehicle was left at a Hyundai dealership in XXXX, Maryland. I did not sign any voluntary surrender or repossession authorization, and I retained no surrender documentation because none was executed. The vehicle was left via a night drop marked for service, not surrendered to the lienholder. 
Hyundai Capital America subsequently took possession of the vehicle and disposed of it at auction, applying the proceeds against the loan and reporting a deficiency balance of approximately {$26000.00}. 
My dispute concerns the following : No voluntary surrender authorization exists. I never signed any document authorizing Hyundai Capital America to take possession of or dispose of the vehicle. 
I did not receive a Notice of Disposition ( Notice of Sale of Vehicle ) as required under Maryland Commercial Law 9-611 and the Maryland Credit Grantor Closed End Credit provisions ( Md. Code Comm. Law 12-1001 et seq. ) prior to the disposition of the collateral. 
The address Hyundai Capital America had on file ( XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX, MD XXXX ) was vacated by me in XX/XX/XXXX, more than a year before the vehicle was disposed of. I received no notice of disposition at any address. Hyundai Capital America had alternative means of contacting me the dealership was in active telephone contact with me yet I was never provided proper notice of the sale, my right to redeem the collateral, or an accounting. 

Under Maryland law, a secured party 's failure to provide proper notice of disposition affects its right to collect a deficiency. A deficiency that is not legally substantiated can not be accurately reported as an owed debt. 
I am requesting that Hyundai Capital America provide : A copy of any signed voluntary surrender or repossession authorization bearing my signature. 
A copy of the Notice of Disposition / Notice of Sale of Vehicle sent prior to the auction, including the specific address it was sent to and proof of mailing. 
An itemized accounting of the auction sale, including the sale price, all fees and charges applied, and the calculation of the deficiency balance. 
Documentation that the disposition was conducted in a commercially reasonable manner as required under Maryland Commercial Law 9-610.

If Hyundai Capital America can not substantiate compliance with Maryland notice and disposition requirements, the reported deficiency balance is not legally substantiated and its reporting on my credit file is inaccurate. I request that the tradeline be deleted from all credit bureau reports.

Issue: Problem with a company's investigation into an existing problem
Consumer complaint narrative:
IN THE MATTER AT HAND, Complainant contends that the information furnished, verified, updated, and repeatedly re-published by Discover Financial Services ( XXXX ) to XXXX XXXX XXXX, and any other Consumer Reporting Agency is facially illogical, patently inaccurate, materially misleading, internally inconsistent, and incapable of reasonable verification as accurate. XXXX has verified and re-verified the disputed information as accurate notwithstanding discordant CRA reporting, contradictory payment-history reporting, incompatible DoFD and delinquency-anchor information, inconsistent obsolescence-derived reporting, and documentary contradictions. Such conduct violates the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), 15 U.S.C. 1681 et seq., and Regulation V, including 12 C.F.R. 1022.42 and Appendix E to Part 1022.

DEFINITIONS 1. Consumer File means a consumers file within the meaning of FCRA 603 ( g ), 15 U.S.C. 1681a ( g ) : all information on that consumer recorded and retained by a Consumer Reporting Agency, regardless of how that information is stored. The term is used to identify the body of information maintained by a Consumer Reporting Agency, including any item of information subject to reinvestigation under FCRA 611 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ), 15 U.S.C. 1681i ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ), and does not imply that a furnisher itself maintains a Consumer File.

2. Consumer Reporting Agency or CRA has the meaning assigned to that term in FCRA 603 ( f ), 15 U.S.C. 1681a ( f ), and includes any person who, for monetary fees, dues, or on a cooperative nonprofit basis, regularly engages in whole or in part in the practice of assembling or evaluating consumer credit information or other information on consumers for the purpose of furnishing consumer reports to third parties, and who uses any means or facility of interstate commerce for the purpose of preparing or furnishing consumer reports. 

3. Furnisher means a person or entity that furnishes information relating to consumers to one or more Consumer Reporting Agencies for inclusion in a consumer report, as that term is used in FCRA 623, 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2, and defined in Regulation V, 12 C.F.R. 1022.41 ( c ).

4. Indirect Dispute means a dispute submitted by a consumer to a Consumer Reporting Agency concerning the completeness or accuracy of information contained in the consumers Consumer File, where the Consumer Reporting Agency provides notice of the dispute to the Furnisher. The term includes disputes that trigger a furnishers duties under FCRA 623 ( b ), 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( b ), after notice from a Consumer Reporting Agency .

5. Direct Dispute means a dispute submitted directly to a Furnisher by a consumer concerning the accuracy of information contained in a consumer report and pertaining to an account or other relationship that the Furnisher has or had with the consumer, within the meaning of Regulation V, 12 C.F.R. 1022.41 ( b ). The term includes disputes governed by 12 C.F.R. 1022.43.

6. Dispute means either a Direct Dispute or an Indirect Dispute, as the context requires.

7. Reinvestigation means a Consumer Reporting Agencys investigation or reinvestigation of disputed information under FCRA 611, 15 U.S.C. 1681i. When used with respect to a Furnisher, the term refers only to the Furnishers investigation, review, correction, deletion, modification, blocking, or reporting obligations after receiving notice of a dispute, and does not imply that the Furnisher is itself a Consumer Reporting Agency.

8. Furnisher Duties means the duties imposed on a Furnisher by FCRA 623, 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2, Regulation V, 12 C.F.R. Part 1022, Subpart E, and any other applicable implementing regulation. 9. 10. 11. 12. 13. Payment History means the month-by-month reporting of an accounts payment performance, including whether each reported month was reported as current, paid as agreed, late, delinquent, charged off, in collection, deferred, in forbearance, transferred, closed, or otherwise assigned a payment rating or status. The term includes any status field, account-condition field, narrative status, account remark, or equivalent reporting that communicates the accounts present or historical credit status.

Issue: Problem with a purchase shown on your statement
Consumer complaint narrative:
During a home renovation in XXXX, I authorized my contractor to use my American Express XXXX card solely for construction materials and services. All legitimate charges appeared on my statements as payments directly to the contractor 's company. Four charges totaling {$62000.00} were made by the contractor to two entirely unrelated vendors a leather goods retailer ( {$16000.00}, XX/XX/year> ) and a home security/automation company ( {$46000.00} total, XXXX XXXX ) without my knowledge or consent. I received no goods or services from either vendor.

The contractor has admitted in writing to using these vendors as alternative payment processors without informing me. When initially asked what the charges were for, he was unable to identify them. He only recently claimed to have " signed invoices '' after months of being unable to produce any documentation which I believe to be fabricated after the fact.

American Express 's handling has been deficient in multiple respects : Fraud case XXXX was opened and closed on the basis that I " released my card number '' to the contractor. This is factually incorrect the contractor already held my card details from months of prior authorized transactions. I made no affirmative decision to share my details with these merchants, and the card remained in my possession at all times. Furthermore, this standard would eliminate American Express 's ability to investigate fraud by any vendor with whom a cardholder has previously conducted a legitimate transaction rendering cardholders entirely unprotected against misuse by any merchant they have ever paid.

Under the Fair Credit Billing Act, unauthorized use is defined as use without actual, implied, or apparent authority. My contractor had authority for construction materials only not for charges at a leather goods store or home security company. These are unauthorized charges by legal definition regardless of whether he previously held my card number.

All four charges were repeatedly rejected as disputes on the basis of a 60-day policy without any substantive human review. Disputes were auto-closed in some cases within minutes of being opened. A disputes specialist manually reopened them with instructions for human review, yet the automated system continued to override that instruction.

The charges were not discoverable within 60 days as they were deliberately obscured within a high volume of authorized construction transactions. Once discovered during a routine financial review, I acted immediately and in good faith. The 60-day rule is American Express 's internal policy, not a legal requirement under the FCBA.

American Express 's own fraud team directed me to consolidate a valid " goods and services not received '' dispute ( XXXX ) into the fraud case. By subsequently closing the fraud case, American Express closed a legitimate dispute without resolution through a process entirely of its own making.

I have comprehensive supporting documentation including the contractor 's written admissions, full account statements showing the anomalous charge pattern, a Stripe refund confirmation that was never honored, and records showing the contractor asked me to misrepresent the charges as " unrecognized '' which I declined. I have submitted two formal written appeals by certified mail and have engaged legal counsel.

I am requesting that the CFPB ensure American Express conducts a proper senior human review of all four charges on their merits, and that the fraud case closure be reconsidered on the basis that the " released card number '' premise does not constitute blanket authorization under the FCBA.

XX/XX/year> : Followed up again. No one could provide information or assistance. A representative suggested writing to the executive board. 

XX/XX/year> : A research team member concluded that the promotion does not apply because " the account ending in the last 4 digits '' supposedly refers to the last four digits of the card used. When I pointed out that " account ending in '' and " card ending in '' are not interchangeable terms in banking, and that authorized users do not have separate accounts, I was told, " this is how it should be interpreted. '' This explanation is unreasonable and inconsistent with industry standards. The promotions language is ambiguous, the interpretation provided is incorrect, and the lack of disclosure has resulted in significant inconvenience and wasted time across multiple months and multiple departments.

Company : Bilt Technologies , Inc. ( Bilt Rewards ) Reference prior complaint : CFPB Complaint ID XXXX ( closed " with explanation, '' company response dated XX/XX/2026 ) Product : Credit card rewards/ rewards travel portal Complaint type : Reopening/ continued harm unresolved financial loss and bad-faith complaint handling -- - 1. Why I am filing again I am filing this new complaint because my prior complaint ( ID XXXX ) was closed " with explanation '' on the basis of a response from Bilt that was materially incomplete and that substituted a technicality for an actual resolution. Bilt 's response argued, in effect, that because its travel portal never produced a confirmed booking, " no travel services were purchased '' and therefore Bilt " does not have a basis to provide reimbursement, '' citing Terms that limit liability for consequential damages.

That reasoning inverts the actual problem. The harm to me was not caused by a completed transaction. * * The harm was caused by Bilt 's product failing silently and repeatedly while Bilt provided no functioning channel to fix it. * * A rewards travel portal that accepts a booking attempt, returns no confirmation, no Trip ID, and no error message, and then offers no accessible support to resolve it, is itself the defect. Bilt 's response treats the absence of a completed booking as its defense, when that absence is precisely the failure I am complaining about.

2. What actually happened ( summary ; fully documented in prior complaint ) Between XX/XX/XXXX and XX/XX/2026, I attempted four times to book a flight for my postpartum wife and our infant son through the Bilt Rewards travel portal so they could travel with her parents on an already-purchased XXXX XXXX  XXXX ( XXXX, departing XX/XX/2026 ). Each attempt including one using approximately XXXX of my Bilt points silently failed : no confirmation, no Trip ID, no error, no notification. Bilt offers no phone support. The only channel was text/chat with human responses exceeding 2448 hours. I sent a written email setting a clear XXXX XXXX PST deadline, warning that I would otherwise be forced to book elsewhere at rising fares. Bilt did not respond by the deadline.

After ten days of failures and price escalation, I was forced to purchase replacement tickets directly through XXXX XXXX so my wife and infant would still have her parents ' support in transit. My out-of-pocket loss, directly caused by Bilt 's platform failures and inaccessible support, was approximately * * {$2500.00} * * ( replacement XXXX XXXX tickets of {$1600.00} plus the now-stranded, non-refundable XXXX XXXX tickets of {$800.00} that the failed booking made unusable as planned ).

3. Why Bilt 's closing response should not have ended this matter Bilt 's XX/XX/2026 response is notable as much for what it omits as for what it argues : - It omits that Bilt 's own VP of Operations and Support personally committed in writing to a resolution and then went silent for over two months.On XX/XX/2026, " XXXX, '' identifying himself as VP of Operations and Support, wrote to me directly acknowledging the failure ( " that's on us '' ) and stating Bilt holds itself " to a high standard. '' I replied the same day with a documented, specific request for resolution. Bilt never responded. A VP-level written commitment to make something right, followed by total silence, is not a good-faith resolution effort and Bilt 's CFPB response conceals that this outreach ever occurred.

- It mischaracterizes the points " courtesy '' as a resolution attempt. On XX/XX/2026, Bilt unilaterally added XXXX points to my account as a " one-time courtesy '' for a documented ~ {$2500.00} cash loss without asking me. When I declined and restated my actual request, Bilt said there was " nothing else we can do, '' and when I asked them to reverse the unrequested points, they removed them within the hour. This sequence an unrequested gesture, immediately withdrawn the moment it was declined was then used as the paper trail to characterize the matter as handled and close it. That is the appearance of resolution without the substance of one.

- It hides behind a " no completed transaction '' technicality and a consequential-damages clause. Bilt can not design a product that fails silently, strip out every effective support channel, ignore a clearly stated deadline, and then disclaim all responsibility on the ground that its own failure means " no service was purchased. '' The injury here was substantial, was not reasonably avoidable by me ( I tried four times and escalated through every channel Bilt offered ), and was not outweighed by any benefit. That is the textbook shape of an unfair practice.

4. The pattern this represents ( UDAAP concern ) I ask the CFPB to consider this not only as my individual loss but as a potential unfair and abusive practice affecting other consumers : a financial-product rewards portal that ( a ) fails to complete transactions without surfacing any error, ( b ) provides no telephone support and multi-day chat-only response times for time-sensitive matters, ( c ) ignores explicit consumer deadlines, and ( d ) resolves disputes by offering unsolicited token " courtesies '' and closing on a liability technicality. If Bilt 's portal silently failed four times for me across ten days, it is reasonable to ask how many other members it has affected.

5. Note on escalation I have already begun documenting and publicly sharing this experience, and I intend to continue doing so on a recurring basis until the matter is formally resolved. I am also prepared to escalate further within Bilt 's executive leadership. I would prefer a direct, good-faith resolution and remain open to a conversation.

Supporting documentation ( available / previously filed ) : booking-attempt timeline ; chat snip confirming no phone support ; email confirming Bilt 's non-response after escalation ; email showing the explicit deadline given to Bilt ; XX/XX/XXXX VP outreach and my same-day reply ; XX/XX/XXXX points add/decline/removal thread ; fare/cost documentation ; and Bilt 's own XX/XX/2026 CFPB response.

The following documentation is required to properly validate this debt, and failure to provide the requested information will result in the removal of the debt from my credit report and cessation of all collection efforts.

Please provide : - The name, address, and contact information of the original creditor.

- The full account number associated with the original credit agreement.

- A copy of the complete transaction history for the account, including all charges, payments, and adjustments made since the inception of the alleged debt.

- Documentation proving that the alleged debt is currently owed and has not been discharged, settled, or written off. If the debt has been sold, assigned, or transferred, you must provide full details of the assignment, including the exact date and nature of the transfer.

# # # 2. Original Agreement/Contract Under 15 U.S.C. 1692g ( a ) ( 2 ), you must provide evidence of the original agreement or contract bearing my signature. This document must include : - A copy of the original signed contract or agreement between myself and the original creditor that specifically identifies the terms, conditions, and payment obligations, as well as the item ( s ) or service ( s ) I am purported to owe for.

- The original purchase agreement or sales contract ( if applicable ) showing that the alleged debt is the result of a lawful, executed transaction.

- Itemized receipts or invoices corresponding to the original contract, clearly listing the charges, products, or services associated with the debt.

- Documentation showing that the interest rate and any fees applied to the debt were agreed upon in the original contract, and that these charges are legally permissible under the law.

- Evidence that the amount of debt is accurate and that there are no errors or illegal charges ( including credit insurance, late fees, or other potentially invalid additions ).

I am filing this formal complaint against Goldman Sachs Bank USA ( operating as Marcus by Goldman Sachs ) regarding an unannounced, abrupt modification to their transaction processing policies. For several consecutive years, I have routinely and successfully paid my monthly credit card balances by initiating external ACH pull requests directly from my credit card issuers, drawn against my Marcus High-Yield Savings Account. I am filing a formal complaint against JPMorgan Chase Bank for violating Federal Regulation E in connection with a series of unauthorized electronic fund transfers made from my Chase checking account. I am a victim of identity theft. A fraudster used my stolen account and routing number to make four unauthorized ACH withdrawals to a merchant listed as XXXX, each for {$210.00}, on XX/XX/year> ; XX/XX/year> ; XX/XX/year> ; and XX/XX/year>, totaling {$840.00}. Chase initially issued provisional credits for three of the payments but later reversed them and denied my claim, asserting that my 60day reporting window began on XX/XX/year>, when the first periodic statement was issued. This interpretation is incorrect and inconsistent with Regulation E.

Second, these transfers were executed using only my stolen account number, not any access device issued to me. Under 12 CFR 1005.6 ( a ), when unauthorized transfers occur through accountnumber fraud rather than a card, PIN, or access device, the consumers liability is XXXX. Because the merchant can not identify me as the customer, the transfers are per se unauthorized under Regulation E. I had no contractual relationship with XXXX, no visibility into the fraudulent account, and no ability to stop or cancel the recurring debits. Chases denial ignores this critical fact. 

Chases investigation was neither reasonable nor compliant with 12 CFR 1005.11. The bank reversed provisional credits without addressing the core evidence : the merchant denies the account exists, the transactions were initiated using stolen account information, and at least one of the transfers was indisputably reported within the required timeframe. Chases position improperly shifts liability onto me despite clear regulatory protections for identitytheft victims and accountnumber fraud cases. I am requesting that Chases compliance management team manually review this file, reverse the reversals, restore the full {$840.00} to my account, and provide written confirmation that the matter has been resolved in accordance with Regulation E.

XX/XX/XXXX Subject : CFPB Complaint ID : XXXX, XXXX Wells Fargo Case Number : XXXX CFPB Complaint Update Concerns Regarding Wells Fargo Safe Deposit Box Investigation Process , Repeated Case Closures, Claimed Authorization Issue, and Credit Card Cancellation Dear CFPB Representative , We respectfully submit this update regarding our ongoing complaint involving missing contents from my XXXX mothers Wells Fargo safe deposit box. 

Our family remains deeply concerned that Wells Fargo has not provided a meaningful, transparent, or independent review of this matter. Instead, Wells Fargo appears to have repeatedly closed or limited complaint reviews, issued boilerplate responses, and redirected responsibility back to the same XXXX branch involved in the events.

The matter was reported to the XXXX branch the same day, and a police report was promptly filed. Since then, our family has submitted extensive documentation, including inventories, affidavits, photographs, receipts, serial numbers, Power of Attorney documents, and supporting explanations. 

One of our major concerns is Wells Fargos repeated position that it did not have permission to share information with the CFPB. My Power of Attorney authorizes me to handle my mothers financial matters and communicate with Wells Fargo on her behalf. In addition, our family filed complaints with the CFPB specifically to request the involvement of the government agency responsible for oversight of consumer financial matters involving banks. 

We understand that Wells Fargo may have internal requirements for authorization. However, Wells Fargo has not clearly identified what specific separate form, signature, or authorization it claims is missing. Instead, the banks repeated closure or limitation of complaint reviews on this basis has the effect of preventing the CFPB from obtaining meaningful information, while leaving our family without substantive answers. 

We respectfully ask the CFPB to require Wells Fargo to clearly identify any specific authorization it claims is needed, rather than allowing Wells Fargo to rely on a vague no permission explanation while avoiding a substantive response. 

Our concern is that Wells Fargos handling has not addressed the substance of the complaint. Specifically : 1. Wells Fargo has repeatedly closed or limited complaint reviews while stating that it did not have permission to share information with the CFPB ; 2. Our family has submitted Power of Attorney documents and has attempted to cooperate fully ; 3. Our family filed CFPB complaints to request government oversight and involvement ; 4. Wells Fargo has not clearly identified what exact additional document, form, or signature is supposedly needed ; 5. The repeated closures have the effect of preventing the CFPB from obtaining information from Wells Fargo ; 6. Wells Fargo continues to direct safe deposit box questions back to the Houston XXXX XXXX, while the branch has not provided any investigation updates to our family. 

We are also concerned that the investigation does not appear sufficiently independent. The alleged loss occurred in connection with a safe deposit box at the branch, yet Wells Fargo continues to indicate that the branch is handling the claim directly. We respectfully believe that a matter involving alleged missing contents from a bank-controlled safe deposit environment should receive independent review by personnel or departments outside the branch directly involved. 

Another serious concern is Wells Fargos slow and incomplete cooperation with law enforcement. The branch provided safe deposit box vault entry records to our family and the police but has not provided any surveillance videos and names of the staff members who assisted us with vault access during relevant visits. Wells Fargo should have records identifying which employees serviced customers at the vault. In a police investigation involving alleged missing safe deposit box contents, those records are highly relevant. 

In addition to the safe deposit box matter, Wells Fargo later cancelled my mothers credit card. The cancellation letter listed reasons that appear inconsistent with my mothers actual financial and payment history. My mother had an excellent credit score at the time of card cancellation ; she also has sufficient equity, income, and savings to pay her debts. She has always paid on time. The particular Wells Fargo credit card that was cancelled reportedly carried no balance since XX/XX/XXXX. Therefore, Wells Fargos statement that her payments were too low relative to the Wells Fargo balance appears unreasonable and troubling. 

We understand Wells Fargo may deny that the credit card cancellation had any connection to the safe deposit box dispute, police report, or CFPB complaint. However, the timing of the cancellation, during an unresolved safe deposit box investigation and active complaint process, creates a reasonable concern of possible adverse treatment after my mothers family raised serious concerns against Wells Fargo. We are not claiming proof of retaliation at this time, but we respectfully believe the timing and circumstances should be reviewed carefully and independently. 

The credit card cancellation significantly affected my mothers credit profile and added additional emotional distress during an already difficult unresolved dispute with Wells Fargo. 

Our concerns are not limited solely to my mothers financial loss. This matter raises broader consumer protection concerns for elderly and vulnerable customers, including senior XXXX customers who may face language or cultural barriers and may not know how to defend themselves when valuables go missing from a safe deposit box they believed was protected by a major financial institution. 

We respectfully request that the CFPB ask Wells Fargo to : 1. Explain why the complaint has been repeatedly closed or limited without meaningful findings ; 2. I am a Citibank customer of approximately 29 years ; my primary joint checking account ( ending XXXX ) has been open continuously since XXXX. The closure was not the result of any failure to cooperate on my part. The KYC review opened around XX/XX/XXXX. Because my assigned financial advisor ( XXXX XXXX ) failed to advance the process, I personally called Citi 's KYC department on at least three occasions ( XX/XX/XXXX, XX/XX/XXXX, and XX/XX/XXXX ) and provided every item requested. On these calls I : - Corrected inaccurate information in Citi 's own KYC profile, including a long-dissolved former employer ( XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX which ceased operations in XXXX ) and a phantom company ( " XXXX XXXX '' ) that Citi had listed as my source of wealth. The correct entity is XXXX XXXX XXXX, my own registered LLC.

- Provided detailed source-of-wealth information and, at Citi 's request, supplied statements from external retirement and brokerage accounts to substantiate that my Citi holdings were consistent with my stated net worth.

- Was told by Citi 's KYC representatives that the review was essentially complete and that no further action was required from me. 

Despite this, Citi issued a closure-warning letter dated XX/XX/XXXX ( closure date XX/XX/XXXX ) and ultimately closed all of my accounts. On XX/XX/XXXX, my Citi Wealth Relationship XXXX emailed me acknowledging that I had been " incredibly cooperative and transparent, '' stating that the closure was unexpected, and confirming that she had escalated the matter to KYC management to seek reopening. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, two members of Citi 's Florida wealth-management leadership called me directly and acknowledged, on a recorded Citi line , that the closure of my accounts was caused by a defect in Citi 's own systems and not by any failure on my part. They confirmed I had cooperated and provided the requested information " each and every time, '' and stated that my accounts were closed even though I had done so. They described this as a recurring " glitch '' in Citi 's systems that they are actively working to repair, stated that it is affecting " far too many '' Citi customers across multiple business lines including Citi Private Bank, and said they had escalated the problem that day to senior Citi operations leadership. They called the treatment of a 29-year relationship " inexcusable, '' and offered to attempt to re-establish my accounts and reverse the resulting charges. XXXX XXXX also committed to send me a written follow-up. This was a management-level admission that my accounts were wrongfully closed by a known, systemic process failure, not for any legitimate compliance reason.

Citi has only partly honored those commitments, and its internal handling remains contradictory. As of the date of this complaint, Citibank has reopened my primary 29-year joint checking account ( ending XXXX ), which I can again use. That reopening, however, was incomplete and left the account functionally impaired by the same systems Citi 's management has admitted are defective : my ATM/debit cards were never reinstated and remained blocked even after the accounts were reopened a defect Citibank discovered only when I happened to flag it on XX/XX/XXXX and my household was silently dropped from the account 's subscription-rebate ( perks ) benefit program when Citi 's system closed and reopened the accounts. Both had to be corrected manually after the fact. The second checking account ( ending XXXX ) remains closed ; it existed only to link my departing IRA, so I do not seek its restoration. The XXXX XXXX account ( ending XXXX ) is open but unfunded. XXXX XXXX never sent the written follow-up or the direct contact information he committed to provide on XX/XX/XXXX, now more than a week ago. On XX/XX/XXXX, two Citi units gave me directly contradictory information on the same day. My wealth relationship manager 's office emailed asking me to re-document my " source of wealth '' on a business questionnaire, while Citi 's KYC department confirmed to me on a recorded call that my source of wealth had already been accepted in XXXX and that the review was " satisfied/approved '' on XX/XX/XXXX with " nothing else needed. '' Closure-related charges have continued, and the disruption from the wrongful closure of a XXXX relationship remains ongoing and unremedied. 

That same evening ( XX/XX/XXXX ), Citibank restricted every one of my accounts again under a new case reference ( XXXX ), hours after its own KYC department had confirmed on a recorded line that the prior review was satisfied and there was no block. The restriction bars deposits, transfers, and withdrawals from my bank accounts and warns that if I do not act, Citibank will liquidate my retirement account and mail me a check. The restriction notice states that my accounts were restricted because I " have not yet provided critical, missing information, '' frames the restriction as something I can " easily lift '' by providing that information, and presents closure as avoidable by a XX/XX/XXXX deadline. It presents the restriction, in other words, as a conditional and preventable consequence within my control. That stated basis is false on Citi 's own record. Citi 's KYC department confirmed on a recorded call the same day that I had already provided the information, that it was accepted in XXXX, and that there was " no block. '' And on XX/XX/XXXX, my own Citi relationship manager confirmed to me in writing that the restriction is procedural, that the case is simply being finalized internally, and that there is " no new needed information '' from me. Citibank nonetheless imposed the full restriction immediately, on a stated basis its own employees had already disproved. The adverse action was taken first. It was not a future consequence I could avert by supplying anything, because Citi confirms there is nothing left for me to supply. 

Citibank subsequently lifted the restriction on my deposit accounts my joint checking was usable again within days yet it has continued to generate and mail me the same restriction notices. A mailed copy of the XX/XX/XXXX restriction notice reached me about a week later, on or about XX/XX/XXXX. When I called Citibank about it, a representative told me that no further information was needed, that the case was simply being finalized, and that Citibank 's system " will periodically continue to send notices until the case is closed, '' so I should " disregard '' the notice. Citibank is thus mailing a 29-year customer formal notices that state he failed to provide " critical, missing information '' and threaten to liquidate his retirement account, while simultaneously instructing him to ignore those notices because nothing is in fact outstanding. A consumer can not reliably tell a genuine restriction notice from XXXX Citibank will later say to disregard. 

This was still unresolved as of XX/XX/XXXX. Roughly two weeks after Citibank 's representatives first told me the review was in its " final stages, '' I called Citibank 's KYC department again to confirm my status. A representative told me my accounts were unblocked, but that the review remained open and was in a " disposition '' stage that had been handed to another Citibank department for a final approval she could neither see nor expedite, with no further information needed from me. She again offered to request a written " KYC satisfied '' letter once the review closes a letter I have asked for repeatedly and still do not have. To date, Citibank has never rescinded its XX/XX/XXXX restriction notice in writing. That notice still states on its face that my Citi accounts will be closed, and my retirement account liquidated and mailed to me as a check, if I do not provide information by XX/XX/XXXX the very notice Citibank 's representatives have told me to disregard because nothing is in fact outstanding. More than two weeks after Citibank 's personnel began telling me the matter was in its " final stages, '' Citibank still has not given me a single authoritative written answer reconciling that standing closure-and-liquidation notice with its assurances that I owe it nothing further.

Underlying every step of this is a single, systemic failure : Citibank 's automated KYC and account-closure processes took adverse action against a fully compliant 29-year customer, repeated it, and would not release it and no person at Citibank has been able to stop or override it. My assigned financial advisor wrote to me that the closure was " beyond our control. '' My relationship manager advocated for me for weeks, including on weekends and after hours, yet the restriction persisted and the false notices kept arriving. Citibank 's own Florida wealth-management leadership admitted the closure was a system defect, said they had escalated it to senior bank-operations leadership, and still could neither prevent the renewed restriction nor stop Citibank 's systems from mailing me notices they themselves told me to disregard to the point that, in XXXX XXXX, a senior Citibank manager was reduced to escalating internally to try to switch off the bank 's automated " missing information '' messages, which the system continued to generate by default. When a bank 's own advisor, relationship manager, and senior management all acknowledge the customer did nothing wrong and still can not stop the bank 's systems from closing his accounts, freezing his retirement assets, and mailing him false liquidation threats, the failure is systemic not the error of any one employee.

I am asking the CFPB to require Citibank to : ( 1 ) produce the recordings of my XX/XX/XXXX, XX/XX/XXXX, and XX/XX/XXXX KYC calls under Reference ID XXXX, and the XX/XX/XXXX call from its wealth-management leadership ; ( 2 ) explain the basis for closing and then restricting my accounts after its own representatives confirmed my compliance and after its own management attributed the closure to a system defect, including how it could restrict my accounts for " missing information '' that its own KYC department confirmed on a recorded call the same day, and that its own relationship manager confirmed in writing on XX/XX/XXXX, had already been provided and accepted ; ( 3 ) reverse any fees or third-party charges ( e.g., stop-payment fees ) caused by the closure ; ( 4 ) correct the inaccurate source-of-wealth/employment records that drove the adverse action ; and ( 5 ) given Citi management 's own statement that this defect is affecting " far too many '' customers, examine whether other consumers have been subjected to the same wrongful closures.

I am submitting this complaint regarding what I believe to be unfair and deceptive practices by Rocket Mortgage in connection with a loan recast request. 

In XXXX, I made approximately {$110000.00} in additional principal payments toward my mortgage loan. Recently, I contacted Rocket Mortgage to inquire about recasting the loan to reflect the reduced principal balance. During my initial call, the representative was able to calculate within seconds what my new principal and interest payment would be if the loan were recast. The reduction would have lowered my monthly payment by more than {$700.00}. I was informed there would be a one time {$250.00} recast fee. While I consider that fee excessive given the minimal administrative effort involved, I understand it is disclosed in their terms. 

I told the representative I needed time to consider the request and would call back. 

When I called back to proceed, the representative immediately processed the {$250.00} fee. Only after charging the fee did he inform me that the recast would take 30 to 45 days to take effect and that my payment would not be reduced until XX/XX/XXXX. This timing means I will be required to make two additional higher monthly payments despite the fact that the principal reduction has already occurred and Rocket is able to calculate the new payment instantly.

This delay was not disclosed up front before the fee was charged. Had I been told clearly and explicitly that the payment reduction would not take effect for 30 to 45 days, I would have reconsidered whether to proceed at that time. The representatives failure to disclose this material information before processing the fee is deceptive.

More broadly, the practice itself appears unfair. Rocket Mortgage can determine the new payment amount in seconds. There is no legitimate reason for borrowers to be required to continue making inflated payments for 30 to 45 days after paying a fee for a recast, particularly when the reduced principal balance is already reflected on the loan. This results in consumers paying additional interest that could easily be avoided if the recast were implemented promptly. 

I am requesting that the CFPB investigate Rocket Mortgages recast practices, including their disclosure of implementation timelines and the reasonableness of the delay in applying payment reductions after collecting recast fees.

Copies of any signed agreements, contracts, applications, or documents bearing my signature.

I believe the use of documents that contain these date discrepancies or that may not have been properly executed could mislead consumers and courts regarding the ownership and legal status of a debt. I believe this conduct may implicate provisions of the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, including 15 U.S.C. 1692e, 1692e ( 2 ) ( A ), 1692e ( 10 ), and 1692f, which prohibit false, deceptive, misleading, unfair, or unconscionable debt collection practices. 

I have attached copies of the Affidavit of Debt, Bill of Sale, and related court documents showing the dates that form the basis of my complaint. I respectfully request that the CFPB investigate whether XXXX  and HAYT, HAYT, & LANDAU, P.L. used inaccurate or misleading documentation in connection with collecting this alleged debt.

Issue: Advertising and marketing, including promotional offers
Consumer complaint narrative:
I am submitting a consumer complaint regarding the annual Companion Certificate benefit marketed with the XXXX XXXX XXXX American Express credit card. 

My concern is not that the benefit does not exist, but that the way it is marketed creates a consumer expectation that does not match the real-world ability to use the benefit. I believe this may constitute misleading or deceptive marketing.

The card is promoted with language implying that cardholders can bring a companion for free each year. This benefit is prominently featured as a primary justification for the cards annual fee. However, after becoming a cardholder and attempting to redeem the certificate, I discovered that the real-world limitations are far more restrictive than a typical consumer would reasonably expect.

Key issues experienced : The certificate can only be used on a very limited subset of fare classes, which are often unavailable on many flights and routes.

All flight segments in a multi-segment itinerary must have this limited fare inventory available, which dramatically reduces usable options.

Travel must be round-trip and completed before expiration, further reducing flexibility.

Alaska residents face additional practical barriers due to routing limitations and limited flight inventory from smaller markets.

The certificate often can not be used during peak or typical vacation travel periods when most consumers would naturally expect to travel.

Many consumers, including myself, experience repeated failed searches and ultimately risk certificate expiration due to lack of qualifying flights.

While these limitations are disclosed in the fine print, they are not presented with comparable prominence to the headline marketing message. The marketing creates a strong impression of a broadly usable annual companion ticket, while the actual redemption process is highly constrained and difficult for many consumers to use successfully.

This creates a material gap between the perceived value used to justify the annual fee and the practical usability of the benefit.

I respectfully request that this promotion be reviewed for potentially misleading marketing practices, particularly regarding : The prominence and clarity of limitations The real-world usability of the advertised benefit Whether the average consumer would reasonably understand the redemption difficulty before applying for the card Thank you for your time and for reviewing this concern.

I am submitting this follow-up complaint regarding Wells Fargos handling of multiple unauthorized electronic fund transfer ( EFT ) disputes, the resulting overdraft balance, and the closure of my checking account. 

I previously filed complaints regarding unauthorized transactions that I did not authorize, initiate, participate in, or benefit from. Wells Fargo responded but failed to adequately address several important issues regarding the investigation and denial of these claims. 

The disputed transactions included : - Claim XXXX : {$900.00} XXXX transaction disputed on XX/XX/XXXX and denied on XX/XX/XXXX - Claim XXXX : {$140.00} XXXX XXXX transaction disputed on XX/XX/XXXX and denied the same day - Claim XXXX : {$200.00} XXXX XXXX XXXX transaction disputed on XX/XX/XXXX and later denied after provisional credit reversal - Claim XXXX : unauthorized recurring payments totaling {$92.00}, initially denied and later reversed after additional review and credited back on XX/XX/XXXX My disputes consistently involved claims of unauthorized transactions and fraud. However, Wells Fargos denial explanations repeatedly referenced concepts such as : - failure to return merchandise, - no indication services differed from the merchant description, - or failure to revoke authorization in a timely manner. 

These explanations do not address my actual disputes, which were that certain transactions themselves were unauthorized. 

Most concerning is the {$900.00} XXXX transaction. I did not authorize this transaction, did not conduct business with XXXX, did not receive any benefit from the transaction, and have never shopped there. Wells Fargos response failed to explain what evidence was relied upon to conclude that the transaction was authorized. 

Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E, financial institutions are required to conduct reasonable investigations into alleged unauthorized EFTs. Under 15 U.S.C. 1693g ( b ), the burden of proof is on the financial institution to establish that the transfers were authorized. 

Importantly, Wells Fargo later overturned one previously denied claim after additional review and recredited my account for {$92.00} on XX/XX/XXXX. This demonstrates that at least one prior investigation result was inaccurate and raises concerns regarding the reliability and adequacy of the investigations performed on the remaining denied claims. 

The disputed transactions contributed directly to the accounts negative balance and eventual closure. Wells Fargo closed the account on XX/XX/XXXX while disputed unauthorized transaction balances remained unresolved. I do not believe consumers should be required to pay overdraft balances and fees arising from disputed unauthorized transactions before the institution adequately proves authorization. 

Wells Fargo also stated that it reported the account to XXXX XXXX XXXX and internal recovery systems. I am concerned that disputed balances tied to unresolved unauthorized transaction claims are continuing to affect my ability to access banking services. 

I am requesting CFPB review regarding whether Wells Fargo : - Conducted reasonable investigations under Regulation E - Properly satisfied its burden of proving authorization under 15 U.S.C. 1693g ( b ) - Improperly treated unauthorized EFT disputes as merchant or merchandise disputes- Improperly reversed provisional credits without sufficient proof of authorization - Improperly maintained overdraft balances and fees arising from disputed unauthorized transactions - Improperly closed the account while disputed unauthorized transactions remained unresolved - Improperly reported disputed balances to XXXX XXXX XXXX or related systems

What steps Planet will take to ensure borrowers who clearly designate payments as principal-only are not misclassified as payoff borrowers or pressured into sending additional funds unnecessarily.

My goal is for Planet Home Lending to review this process and ensure that future borrowers are clearly informed of their options when making a principal-only payment, especially when the payment is large. A principal-only payment should not be automatically treated as a payoff when the borrowers written instructions say otherwise.

Attachment 1 shows the first wire request for {$140000.00}, which was marked Apply to Principal. Attachment 2 shows the second wire request for {$4400.00}, which was marked Apply to Payoff. Consumer complaint narrative:
To whom it XXXX concern, I am writing to dispute the Claim ID XXXX for {$53.00} opened on XX/XX/year>. The merchandise received is different from the merchant 's description and is defective/unfit for its intended purpose. 

Summary of Misrepresentation : The merchants website advertises this " XXXX XXXX '' using images that depict a roll of flexible tape. Based on these professional images, a consumer reasonably expects a product with the properties of tapespecifically flexibility and adhesion. However, the product received is functionally useless : The product page for the " XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX '' presents a fundamental conflict between its marketing title and technical specifications. While the title prominently uses the word " Metallic, '' which implies a high-sheen, reflective, and brilliant finish, the body text contradicts this by describing a " soft satin finish. '' In the context of professional cake decorating, these terms represent two entirely different aesthetic tiers. A bank claim can be supported by the argument of Material Misrepresentation, as the merchant used a high-value descriptive keyword to trigger a sale while delivering a product that lacks the primary light-reflective properties promised in the heading. 

Furthermore, there is a significant discrepancy regarding the product 's structural performance. The primary marketing photograph depicts the ribbon as a rigid or semi-rigid material capable of holding sharp, upright loops and architectural folds on a cake. Conversely, the description labels the material as " soft and flexible '' edible lace. Physics dictates that a soft, lace-like material can not maintain the structural integrity shown in the photo without internal support, which is not mentioned. This constitutes Deceptive Visual Advertising, as the consumer is induced to purchase based on a " structural '' use case that the actual physical material is incapable of performing.

The listing further fails the consumer by utilizing subjective terminology in place of technical dimensions. By labeling the ribbon as " Wide '' without providing specific measurements in inches or millimeters, the merchant creates a " dimensional ambiguity '' that makes it impossible for a professional to determine if the item is fit for their specific project. In banking disputes, this is categorized as a Failure of Disclosure. Without exact specifications, the term " Wide '' is a subjective claim rather than a factual description, leading to a purchase of an item that may not meet the necessary physical requirements for the intended application.

Transparency regarding safety is also a major fault, as the page lacks a visible ingredient list or allergy warning. For an edible product, particularly one using black and metallic pigments, which often contain iron oxides or specific dyes ( like Red 40 ), the omission of this data is a critical safety gap. The bank 's argument for Non-Disclosure of Essential Safety Information is highly effective here ; a consumer can not be expected to accept an " edible '' product if they can not verify its contents against dietary restrictions or legal food safety standards prior to the transaction.

Finally, the merchant employs a restrictive " No Returns '' policy for food items, which conflicts with their categorization of the item as " Equipment and Supplies. '' This creates a " Liability Shield '' where the merchant avoids accountability for the products failure to perform, like the equipment shown in the photos. A bank claim can argue that this is an Unfair Trade Practice, as the merchant is using the " food '' classification to bypass consumer protection rights when the product fails to meet the " professional grade '' quality standards they advertised. By proving the product is materially different from its description, the merchants " No Return '' policy becomes legally unenforceable in a dispute.

1. Misleading " Metallic '' Representation The primary selling point is the " Metallic '' finish, but the merchant includes a contradictory fine-print disclaimer.

The Critique : The product name explicitly uses the word " Metallic, '' yet the description admits it is " not as metallic '' as their other products and compares it to a " soft satin ''. This is a bait-and-switch tactic where the title promises a high-shine finish that the merchant knows the product can not achieve.

My argument : " The merchant 's own documentation admits the product does not meet the standard defined by its own title. This is deceptive advertising. '' 2. Unfair " No Returns '' Policy for Defective Goods Evil Cake Genius typically refuses returns on edible items regardless of quality.

The Critique : Consumer protection laws generally state that a " No Returns '' policy can not apply to items that are defective or misrepresented.

My argument : " I attempted a good-faith resolution, but the merchant used a blanket 'all sales final ' policy to avoid responsibility for a misrepresented and defective product. '' 3. The " Fit for Purpose '' Failure ( Technical Performance ) The product is marketed as a professional cake decorating tool. However, " Metallic '' food products often require specific chemical compositions to hold their shine.

The Critique : If the ribbon arrives brittle, cracks when bent, or the " metallic '' pigment rubs off on your hands or the cake frosting, it is technically defective.

My argument : " The product is advertised for professional cake application, but its physical properties ( brittleness/pigment transfer ) make it impossible to apply to a curved surface without failure. Under Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ) guidelines, the product fails the 'implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose. ' '' 4. Discrepancy Between Promotional Photos and Reality The photos on the Evil Cake Genius website show a flawless, high-gloss finish.

The Critique : Most bank dispute departments look for a " What I Ordered vs. What I Got '' comparison. If the ribbon looks like matte plastic or dark grey rather than " Metallic Black, '' I should claim Visual Misrepresentation.

My argument : " The merchants marketing materials use edited or enhanced photography to depict a high-gloss metallic finish that is physically impossible to achieve with the actual product provided. This constitutes a material misrepresentation of the goods. '' 5. Violation of the " Implied Warranty of Merchantability. '' Under the Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ), goods sold by a merchant must be " merchantable, '' meaning they must pass without objection in the trade under the contract description.

The Critique : A professional-grade edible ribbon that contains recurring glued seams every 30 inches is not " standard '' for high-end cake design, where a seamless appearance is the core requirement.

My argument : " The product is commercially defective for its advertised purpose. In the cake decorating trade, a ribbon with visible seams every few feet is considered a 'second ' or defective item, yet it was sold at a premium price without prominent disclosure of these defects ''.

6. Violation of the " Implied Warranty of Merchantability '' Under the Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ), goods sold by a merchant must be " merchantable, '' meaning they must pass without objection in the trade under the contract description.

The Critique : A professional-grade edible ribbon that contains recurring glued seams every 30 inches is not " standard '' for high-end cake design, where a seamless appearance is the core requirement.

My argument : " The product is commercially defective for its advertised purpose. In the cake decorating trade, a ribbon with visible seams every few feet is considered a 'second ' or defective item, yet it was sold at a premium price without prominent disclosure of these defects ''.

7. " Bait and Switch '' on Material Quality The Critique : The product is titled " Metallic Black Wide, '' but the description admits it is " not as metallic '' as other products. Using a primary keyword like " Metallic '' while burying a disclaimer that contradicts that very keyword is a classic " bait and switch ''.

My argument : " The merchant used a specific, desirable material quality ( 'Metallic ' ) to induce the sale, while simultaneously acknowledging in the fine print that the product does not possess that quality to a standard degree. This is a material misrepresentation of fact ''.

8. Failure of " Duty of Disclosure '' ( The Hidden Seams ) In professional decorating, a " roll '' implies a continuous, unbroken strip.

The Critique : The merchant hides the fact that this is not one continuous 26-foot ribbon, but multiple short strips glued together. By not placing " SEAMED RIBBON '' in the product title, they are withholding a material fact that would have prevented the purchase.

My argument : " The merchant failed their duty of disclosure. A '26-foot roll ' in a professional context implies a continuous length. The presence of hidden adhesive joints every 30 inches is a manufacturing shortcut that was intentionally omitted from the product 's primary description to mislead the buyer. '' 9. Failure of " Duty of Disclosure '' ( The Hidden Seams ) In professional decorating, a " roll '' implies a continuous, unbroken strip.

The Critique : The merchant hides the fact that this is not one continuous 26-foot ribbon, but multiple short strips glued together. By not placing " SEAMED RIBBON '' in the product title, they are withholding a material fact that would have prevented the purchase.

My argument : " The merchant failed their duty of disclosure. A '26-foot roll ' in a professional context implies a continuous length. The presence of hidden adhesive joints every 30 inches is a manufacturing shortcut that was intentionally omitted from the product 's primary description to mislead the buyer. '' 10. Violation of " Truth in Advertising '' ( The Metallic Lie ) The Critique : The merchant uses a photo that appears to have a high-gloss, reflective sheen ( likely edited or taken under studio lighting that the product can't replicate ).

My argument : " The merchants website uses digitally enhanced imagery to represent a metallic finish that the actual productby the merchant 's own admission in the fine printdoes not possess. This is a violation of FTC Truth in Advertising standards, as the visual representation is the primary basis for the consumer 's purchase decision. '' 11. Breach of " Express Warranty. '' An express warranty is created when a seller makes a specific promise about a product that becomes the " basis of the bargain. '' The Critique : The website claims this product is a " food miracle '' that " behaves like real ribbon. '' If the product snaps, doesn't drape, or has rough, glued edges, they have breached an express warranty.

My argument : " The merchant made specific, high-level performance claims ( e.g., 'behaves like real ribbon ' ) to justify a premium price. The actual product lacks the tensile strength and flexibility of ribbon. Under the Uniform Commercial Code 2-313, the merchant has breached an express warranty, rendering the sale invalid. '' 12. Failure of " Quantity and Continuity. '' In the world of textiles and trims, a " roll '' has a specific meaning.

The Critique : When a consumer buys a " 26-foot roll, '' they are paying for uninterrupted length. Selling a series of 30-inch scraps glued together without clearly labeling the product as " pieced '' or " seamed '' is a failure to deliver the quantity of continuous material expected.

My argument : " The merchant delivered a 'pieced ' product rather than a continuous roll. This is the equivalent of ordering a single 10-foot piece of lumber and receiving five 2-foot pieces glued together. The structural and aesthetic integrity is compromised, and the 'quantity ' of continuous material ordered was never delivered. '' 13. " Unconscionable '' Terms of Service The Critique : The merchant uses a " No Returns '' policy for food items. However, since the item is a pre-manufactured, shelf-stable decorating supply ( not a fresh cake ), the " perishable '' excuse is a legal stretch used to trap customers with defective goods.

My argument : " The merchant 's 'No Returns ' policy is unconscionable when applied to misrepresented or defective non-perishable supplies. Using a 'food ' classification to avoid the Fair Credit Billing Act requirements for 'goods not as described ' is a bad-faith business practice designed to deny consumers their right to a remedy for faulty merchandise. '' 14. Chemical Flavor Profile : The product relies heavily on sodium benzoate, potassium sorbate, and artificial flavors. These preservatives, when paired with high concentrations of black food dye, often produce a bitter, metallic, or soap-like aftertaste that is common in " jet black '' food products.

Plastic-Like Texture : The ribbon contains sodium carboxymethylcellulose and xanthan gum. While these make the ribbon flexible like fabric, they can create a texture that decorators describe as " stretchy like slime '' or " chewy like plastic ''. If it doesn't dissolve like food, it is a failure of " merchantability. '' The " Metallic '' Bitterness : The metallic version specifically adds mica pearlescent pigments. Mica-based additives can impart a gritty or harsh mineral taste that is not " neutral '' or " sweet '' as promised.

15. Zero Adhesion : Despite appearing like a roll of tape, the ribbon has no adhesive properties. The surface is " slippery '' and repels moisture. I tested several liquids ( water and saliva ) to activate a bond, but the material remained non-sticky and failed to adhere to the target surface.

16. Lack of Material Integrity : The item 's texture is comparable to dried chewing gum. It lacks any tensile strength ; pulling even slightly from the edge causes the material to rip randomly in the center rather than unrolling or stretching as a ribbon should.

17. Total Lack of Flexibility : Because the material is brittle and " dry, '' it can not be manipulated or applied to a cake without shattering, making it a " total loss '' product.

Merchant 's Refusal to Cooperate : I contacted the merchant to report these defects and explicitly offered to return the unused portion of the product for a refund. The merchant has refused to resolve the issue or provide a refund for this defective merchandise.

Request for Action : Under the terms of the Fair Credit Billing Act ( and/or [ Visa/Mastercard ] dispute rules for " Goods Not as Described or Defective '' ), I am entitled to a refund. Since the merchant has refused a return and the product is fundamentally defective, I request a full chargeback of the transaction amount.

Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter.

The reversal of {$360.00} caused my account to go negative, which resulted in two overdraft fees of {$35.00} each ( {$70.00} total ) charges I would not have incurred had the deposit been properly processed or the provisional credit not been reversed without a thorough investigation. The only notification I received was a push notification through the Wells Fargo mobile app ; I did not see any mailed notice in time, as I was in the middle of relocating.
