I am submitting this complaint regarding serious failures in the mortgage lending and closing process that caused significant and preventable financial harm. On XX/XX/XXXX, I provided tax returns and debt documentation to the lender prior to fully applying for the loan, specifically to confirm eligibility before making irreversible housing decisions. I was initially issued a pre-approval for a conventional mortgage, and the lender was aware from the outset that gifted funds would be required to close. This was reflected in the postpre-approval document checklist, which specifically requested a gift funds letter. I am a single parent and the sole provider for my XXXX child, and the lender was aware that accurate upfront eligibility review was critical before I committed to a move. All parties were also aware from the beginning that my sister was the real estate agent on the transaction. This was openly discussed during offer negotiations, at which time I made clear that my sister was already gifting funds to assist me and that I would not reduce her commission, particularly given that she was helping me relocate from a safety-driven situation involving stalking and a prior physical attack. Despite this information being known and documented from the outset, the lender failed to properly enter the gifted funds into the loan system. This failure was not identified until approximately XXXX days before closing, when the lenders assistant entered the gifted funds and the system fully declined the loan and was unable to generate a pre-approval. Only at that point did it become clear that I had been placed in a loan product for which I did not qualify, and that the file had not been properly underwritten at any earlier stage. By the time this issue was discovered, I had already relied on the lenders representations to secure a tenant for my prior residence, vacate my home, schedule movers, and commit to a closing timeline. This reliance was driven by repeated assurances of eligibility and by my need to relocate with my minor child for safety reasons, which the lender and builder were aware of. Once underwriting review finally occurred only days before closing, the loan was restructured in a compressed timeframe. As a result, I experienced multiple cash-to-close increases, including XXXX increases on the intended day of closing itself, when my belongings were already loaded on a moving truck and I had no practical ability to delay or unwind the transaction. The financial impact was substantial and unexpected : I paid a {$5000.00} binder and was told I would owe an additional {$8300.00} at closing, plus {$19000.00} in planned gift funds from my sister. These funds were represented as sufficient not only to close, but also to pay off existing debts at closing, including a golf cart loan with a balance of approximately {$8600.00} and a credit card balance of approximately {$1200.00}, as part of the approved loan structure. Due to the lenders late discovery that I was in the wrong loan productcaused by the failure to enter the gifted funds disclosed from the beginningand the resulting loan switch, all available funds were required to be applied to the down payment instead, and none of the planned debt payoff occurred. As a result, I was left in a worse post-closing financial position, with higher ongoing monthly obligations, and my available savings were reduced to approximately {$1900.00}, effectively depleting my financial reserves. The lender was aware that I was already absorbing a monthly shortfall on my prior residence due to market conditions as it transitioned to a rental, and that it was critical for this transaction to be structured in a way that left me financially stable after closing. Instead, the lenders errors compounded my financial exposure. I was required to wire {$18000.00} at the last minute, an unexpected increase of {$9600.00} beyond the originally disclosed {$8300.00}. My sister was forced to increase her contribution from {$19000.00} to {$25000.00} due to XXXX late-stage increases. My mother, who was never intended to assist, was forced to wire {$16000.00} at the last minute so that my child and I would not be displaced, creating financial strain on her as well. On the day of closing, a {$4200.00} shortfall also remained unresolved. While I was distressed and attempting to understand how the transaction could proceed, the builders site agentwho was not involved in loan origination or underwritingexpressed concern and made a personal offer to cover the amount once he was paid. This offer was not accepted, and after closing I expressly declined it in writing due to the lenders errors. This interaction reflects the level of distress and pressure present at closing, not any attempt to resolve lending deficiencies through improper means. After I had already signed all of the closing documents on the day of closing, the closing process was stopped when I was informed that the gifted funds could not be shown as coming directly from my sister, despite the fact that all parties had been aware of her role from the outset. At that point, my mother had already wired her own last-minute funds, despite never having been intended as a gift source, due solely to the repeated cash-to-close increases. With the title company and lender present and aware, I was then guided by the lender and title company on how the funds should be routed so that they could be accepted, even though the underlying source of the funds did not change. Specifically, I was instructed that funds already wired from my sister should be returned to her, then wired to my mother, and then wired from my mother to the title company. As a result, the transaction reflects a documented trail of funds moving from the title company back to my sister, then from my sister to my mother, and then from my mother back to the title company as a second wire, in the amount originally provided by my sister. These instructions were given after execution of the documents, under time pressure, as a means of proceeding with the transaction after repeated last-minute cash-to-close increases and the lenders inability to accept the funds as originally sourced. Even after execution of the closing documents, the cash-to-close amount remained inaccurate and required correction before funding could proceed. After closing, the lender issued refunds totaling {$670.00}, characterizing them as technical adjustments. In a written response dated XX/XX/XXXX, the lender also acknowledged that employee access to my financial and IRS accounts using login credentials and multi-factor authentication codes was not consistent with company policy, though no remediation was offered. Had the lender performed timely underwriting review, properly entered the gifted funds disclosed from the beginning, and confirmed loan eligibility at the outset, I would have delayed closing, saved additional funds, avoided placing my prior home into a lease prematurely, and ensured my debt obligations were properly addressed. As a sole parent responsible for a minor child, the harm I experienced was foreseeable and preventable, and by the time these issues were disclosed days before closing, I had no practical choice but to proceed in order to ensure safety and housing stability for my child. I am requesting that the lender be required to address this consumer harm and provide financial restitution to make me whole.

Subject : Defective Foreclosure, False Posting, and Failure to Provide Proof of Sale Complaint Summary I dispute the validity of the foreclosure conducted by XXXX XXXX XXXX.
All substantive responses regarding this matter have been provided through counsel, XXXX XXXX XXXX, which represents XXXX XXXX XXXX.

The foreclosure process is defective, unsupported by required documentation,
and based on unreliable and contradictory representations. A foreclosure sale has been asserted, yet no evidence has been produced to establish that any valid sale occurred.

This complaint should be reviewed in conjunction with my prior CFPB complaint, No. XXXX, as part of an ongoing pattern of foreclosure-related issues.

Key Violations 1. Defective Posting of Notice of Trustees Sale The response provided through Aldridge Pite LLP relies on a posting declaration stating that the Notice of Trustees Sale was posted at the property.

This is directly contradicted by independent records, as shown in Exhibit A, which includes documentation from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX confirming : - No access request was made - No entry was logged - No posting occurred at the property Instead, the notice was placed at the community gate approximately one mile from the property, not at the property itself.

This does not constitute compliant posting.

Failure to properly post the notice calls into question the validity of the foreclosure process.

2. No Proof of Foreclosure Sale The response provided through Aldridge Pite LLP states that a foreclosure sale occurred on XX/XX/year>. 

However, the following has not been provided : - Trustees Deed Upon Sale - Identity of the purchaser - Sale price - Any recorded documentation confirming the sale A foreclosure sale can not be established without these documents. Despite multiple requests, no documentation has been produced to establish that any valid sale occurred.

3. Contradictory and Evasive Representations The response provided through Aldridge Pite LLP asserts that the foreclosure process complied with applicable law, while simultaneously stating that the response : should not be construed as a statement regarding the actions of any other entities.

This is internally inconsistent.

Assertions of statutory compliance necessarily depend on the actions of all parties involved in the foreclosure process. A party can not assert compliance while disclaiming responsibility for the underlying actions required to establish that compliance.

4. Improper Reliance on Third-Party Vendor The posting declaration relied upon appears to have been performed by a third-party vendor.

However : - The trustee has a non-delegable duty to ensure compliance with foreclosure laws - Any inaccurate or false posting remains the responsibility of the trustee The discrepancy reflected in Exhibit A raises serious concerns regarding the accuracy and integrity of the foreclosure process.

5. Lack of Independent Trustee Verification XXXX XXXX XXXX has not provided any direct response or independent verification of the foreclosure process.

All communications have been made through its counsel.

This raises concerns as to whether the trustee independently verified compliance with statutory requirements, or is relying entirely on unverified third-party representations.

A foreclosure can not be considered reliable where the trustee has not independently confirmed the validity of the process.

Regulatory Concerns The conduct described above may constitute : - Misrepresentation of foreclosure compliance - Failure to maintain and provide accurate records - Failure to provide material documentation to the consumer - Potential unfair or deceptive acts or practices ( UDAAP ) Requested Resolution I request that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX. and XXXX XXXX XXXX provide : 1. This timeline directly contradicts the impression created at the time of sale that I was purchasing a normal factory-new XXXX  product with a valid manufacturer warranty. XXXX XXXX never produced actual documentary proof showing the item was factory-new inventory with a valid manufacturer warranty at the time of sale. Instead, the merchant merely claimed the product appeared new. XXXX serial-number records are objective manufacturer records, while the merchant only offered employee opinions and assumptions.

The merchant attempted to rely on the fact that I initially left a positive review shortly after purchase. Capital One never explained why verified manufacturer serial-number records, merchant internal contradictions, call logs, proof of a safety-related replacement, and the merchants own admissions were all supposedly insufficient evidence. Capital One failed to reconcile the obvious contradictions and evidence in this dispute : * XXXX  confirmed the unit was almost eight months out of warranty.

Instead of fairly evaluating this evidence, Capital One repeatedly focused on impossible or unreasonable evidentiary demands while disregarding the verified manufacturer documentation and the merchants own contradictory statements. 

I am requesting that the CFPB review whether Capital One conducted a reasonable investigation into this billing dispute and whether Capital One improperly denied my claim despite substantial evidence of defective and materially misrepresented merchandise.

FDCPA 1692g ( a ) requires ( 1 ) a statement that unless the consumer disputes the validity of the debt within 30 days, the debt will be assumed valid ; ( 2 ) a statement that if the consumer notifies the debt collector in writing within the 30-day period that the debt is disputed, the debt collector will obtain verification and mail it to the consumer; and ( 3 ) a statement that on the consumers written request within the 30-day period, the debt collector will provide the name and address of the original creditor if different from the current creditor. Regulation F, 12 C.F.R. 1006.34, further requires specific itemization ( itemization date, principal at itemization, interest, fees, payments, credits ) and a standardized consumer response framework.

Issue 2 Third-party disclosure through email subject line ( 15 U.S.C. 1692c ( b ) ) The subject line of the XX/XX/year> email " XXXX, info regarding acct XXXX : owned by LVNV Funding LLC '' expressly identifies LVNV Funding LLC, a known debt-buying entity, in plain text, and references an " acct '' ( account ) " owned by '' that entity. Email subject lines are visible in mobile lock-screen previews, notification banners, shared and household devices, employer-monitored email systems, and inbox listings displayed to anyone with access to the screen. The subject line therefore communicates to any third party who sees the notification that the recipient has an account that has been sold to a debt-buying entity, in violation of 1692c ( b ).

Issue 3 Information conditioned on portal authentication does not satisfy delivery requirements The omitted content described in Issue 1 ( 30-day dispute rights, Reg F itemization, consumer response framework ) is not provided in the email and is, at most, available through the " Login '' or " View Your Account '' portal links. To the extent Resurgent will assert that the omitted validation information is made available through portal authentication, that does not satisfy the FDCPA. Section 1692g ( a ) requires the debt collector to " send the consumer a written notice. '' Making the required statutory disclosures conditionally available through portal authentication is not delivery ; it is at most an offer to provide the disclosures upon the consumers further action. The Bureaus Regulation F preamble treats validation as something the debt collector must provide, not something the consumer must retrieve through portal registration or authentication. Louisiana Revised Statutes 29:422 states : Louisiana adopts the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act ( 50 U.S.C. 3901 et seq. ) and makes all SCRA protections fully enforceable within the state.

The statute applies retroactively and prospectively, per Acts 2002, 1st Ex. Sess., No. 57, Section 2.

All benefits, protections, and rights under SCRA apply to all persons called to service in the uniformed services as defined in R.S. 29:403.

This means that Louisiana law requires lenders operating in the state to comply with SCRA protections, including the 6 % interestrate cap, and allows servicemembers to enforce these rights.

Consumer complaint narrative:

XXXX accessed my consumer report despite there being no demonstrated collection relationship between myself and their company. I have not entered into any contract with Midland Credit Management, and they have failed to provide documentation establishing that they lawfully own or were properly assigned the alleged debt. 
Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( 15 U.S.C. 1681b ( a ) ( XXXX ) ( A ) ), a company may only obtain a consumer report if it intends to use the information in connection with the collection of an account of the consumer. XXXX has not produced evidence that such an account exists or that it has legal authority to collect it. 
Additionally, pursuant to 15 U.S.C. 1681e ( b ), furnishers must follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information reported. Reporting a collection account without substantiating ownership and assignment fails this statutory requirement. 
Further, under 15 U.S.C. 1681i ( a ), when a consumer disputes information, a reasonable reinvestigation must be conducted. Automated verification through systems such as XXXX, without producing documentary evidence of ownership, does not satisfy the requirement of a reasonable reinvestigation. 
Courts have recognized that debt buyers must demonstrate competent evidence of ownership and assignment when attempting to collect or report debts. In XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, involving XXXX XXXX XXXX, the court emphasized that a debt buyer must establish that it owns the specific account at issue and has authority to collect it. Generic bills of sale without account-level documentation are insufficient to prove standing or ownership. 
Accordingly, I am formally requesting that Midland Credit Management provide : Complete chain of title / chain of assignment from the original creditor to XXXX. 
A copy of the executed assignment contract transferring my specific account. 
A bill of sale identifying my alleged account by name and account number. 
Documentation establishing the date XXXX acquired the account. 
Documentation demonstrating permissible purpose at the time of accessing my consumer report. 
A copy of the original signed agreement bearing my signature.

CFPB Complaint Narrative Consumer : XXXX XXXX XXXX : XXXX XXXX/ XXXX XXXX XXXX : Discover Bank Product : Credit Card Billing Dispute ( Services Not Rendered ) Amount in Dispute : {$2200.00} Complaint Summary I am submitting this complaint regarding Discover Banks handling of a billing dispute involving non-delivery of contracted website development services by XXXX XXXX. Despite extensive documentation demonstrating material non-performance by the merchant, Discover declined to provide relief after previously advising me that I would retain dispute rights if the services were not delivered. 

This complaint concerns Discovers dispute handling process, my reasonable reliance on Discovers guidance, and Discovers subsequent refusal to substantively evaluate documentation that directly addressed non-delivery under the contract. 



Background and Dispute History In XX/XX/year>, I was charged {$2200.00} by XXXX XXXX for custom website development services. I timely provided all requested onboarding materials, written content, branding direction, and access credentials. After onboarding, I did not receive meaningful communication from the merchant for approximately three and a half weeks, which exceeded the contractual timeline. 

When I followed up, the merchant provided a generic draft website that did not include the agreed-upon content, branding, colors, service descriptions, or written materials that had been discussed and delivered in writing. 

At that point, I disputed the charge with Discover for services not rendered. 

While the dispute was pending, the merchant contacted me, apologized, and proposed an alternative path forward. The merchant stated they would not contest the dispute and suggested restarting the project by reissuing paperwork and recharging the amount so the project could begin again. 

Before taking any action, I contacted Discover to confirm my rights. 



Dispute Process Transparency and Consumer Reliance During this communication, Discover advised me that if the merchant ultimately failed to deliver the contracted services, I would retain recourse provided I documented non-performance. 

Relying on Discovers guidance, I agreed to give the merchant an additional opportunity to perform. I allowed the original charge to stand, did not re-sign new paperwork, and did not restart the transaction, specifically because I relied on Discovers representation that documentation of non-delivery would preserve my dispute rights. 

This reliance directly informed my decision not to initiate a new transaction and instead to document continued non-performance under the existing agreement. 



Satisfaction of Discovers Stated Dispute Condition I subsequently satisfied the condition Discover identified for retaining dispute rights by submitting extensive documentation demonstrating that the merchant did not deliver the services paid for. Despite this showing of non-delivery, Discover declined to reverse the charge without substantively addressing whether the contractual services were, in fact, performed. 

As a result, the issue is no longer whether documentation was provided, but whether Discover meaningfully evaluated documented non-performance after advising that such documentation would preserve dispute rights. 



Continued Non-Performance and Second Dispute Despite being given more than four and a half months in total from onboarding, the merchant still failed to deliver the contracted services. The website was never completed or launched and continued to contain numerous objective deficiencies, including : Failure to incorporate finalized client-provided written content Duplicated and misplaced service descriptions Incorrect factual information Misrepresentation of services offered At that point, I again disputed the charge and submitted a 28-page documentation packet to Discover. This submission included the signed agreement, written communications, finalized service-specific content that was never implemented, screenshots of errors, and evidence demonstrating that the services paid for were not delivered. 



Discovers Handling of the Dispute Despite this documentation, Discover declined to reverse the charge without substantively addressing whether the contracted services were delivered. Discover stated that no new information had been provided, even though the materials submitted directly addressed non-performance under the contract. 

Separately, Discover ruled in my favor on disputes involving improper hosting fees charged by the same merchant, confirming billing irregularities and improper charges related to services that were not delivered. However, Discover did not apply the same standards of non-delivery to the primary website development charge involving the same merchant. 

This dispute does not involve dissatisfaction, design preference, or subjective judgment. It concerns objective non-performance of contracted services that were paid for but not delivered. 



Basis for CFPB Review I relied on Discovers guidance that documentation of non-performance would preserve my dispute rights. I acted reasonably and in good faith by documenting non-delivery rather than restarting the transaction. Discovers refusal to meaningfully evaluate that documentation, while simultaneously acknowledging improper billing by the same merchant in related disputes, raises concerns regarding the fairness, consistency, and transparency of Discovers dispute handling process. 



Resolution Requested Regulatory Standard Under applicable card network rules and consumer protection standards, a charge for services may be reversed when the merchant fails to deliver the contracted services as agreed, and documentation demonstrating non-delivery must be substantively evaluated. 



Relief Requested I am requesting regulatory review of Discovers dispute handling process and appropriate relief consistent with services not rendered, including reversal of the disputed charge or other corrective action deemed appropriate.

Subject : Complaint Regarding Improper Foreclosure-Related Solicitation, Unannounced Property Access Attempt, Escalation of Possession Demands, and Reliance on XXXX Foreclosure Activity I am submitting this complaint regarding serious concerns involving foreclosure-related solicitation activity, unannounced property access attempts, escalating possession demands, and representations connected to a disputed foreclosure involving my property. 

This complaint should be reviewed in conjunction with prior complaints already submitted regarding the underlying foreclosure process and related foreclosure participants. The conduct described here arose from and relied upon the disputed foreclosure activity already reported. 

On or around XX/XX/year>, a man arrived at the property without prior notice, appointment, authorization, or written consent. He spoke to my husband and stated that his client was interested in purchasing the property and wanted to see the home before placing a bid in what he described as a second bidding period scheduled for XX/XX/year>. 

At that time, my husband clearly informed him that : - the property was not voluntarily being sold, - the foreclosure process was actively disputed, - there were unresolved legal and procedural issues involving the lender and foreclosure process, - and that any party considering purchase should understand the property was involved in ongoing disputes and litigation-related matters. 

Despite this, communications continued. 

Shortly afterward, we received a letter dated XX/XX/year>, asserting that an alleged foreclosure sale occurred on XX/XX/year>. The letter discussed bidding activity, surplus funds, and efforts to increase bids connected to the property. The communication also referenced additional bidding periods and encouraged cooperation to facilitate higher bidding activity. 

Then, on XX/XX/year>, we received additional letters via XXXX asserting that the senders client was now the new owner of the property and requesting that we voluntarily vacate the property in exchange for cash for keys in order to avoid the eviction process. 

The XX/XX/year> letter specifically claimed that a XXXXXXXX XXXX evidencing the alleged purchaser as the officially new owner was attached. However, no Trustees Deed Upon Sale was actually attached to the correspondence. 

This omission is significant because the letters repeatedly asserted ownership rights, possession expectations, urgency to vacate the property, and implied authority over the property while simultaneously failing to provide the very document allegedly evidencing the transfer of title. 

These communications raise serious concerns for several reasons : XXXX. Unannounced Property Visit and XXXX Concerns A representative appeared at the property without prior written authorization or consent while the foreclosure itself remained disputed. This created significant distress and raised concerns regarding trespassing, privacy, and improper interference during an active foreclosure dispute. 

XXXX. Escalation of Possession Claims During an Ongoing Dispute The communications rapidly escalated from : - requesting access to view the property, - to discussing bidding strategies, - to asserting ownership, - to pressuring occupants to vacate under threat of eviction. 

This occurred despite continuing unresolved disputes involving the foreclosure process itself, including issues concerning foreclosure procedures, notice compliance, servicing conduct, accounting concerns, sale verification, and disputed foreclosure-related representations. 

XXXX. Failure to Provide Supporting Ownership Documentation The XX/XX/year> letter represented that a XXXX XXXX Upon Sale was attached and that the purchaser was officially the new owner of the property. However : - no XXXX XXXX Upon Sale was included, - no recorded transfer documentation was provided, - no official recording information was identified, - and no supporting evidence establishing completed transfer of title accompanied the demand for possession-related cooperation. 

Despite this lack of documentation, the letters still advanced ownership assertions and encouraged us to vacate the property voluntarily. 

XXXX. Significant Equity Loss and Financial Harm The property is believed to have an estimated market value in the approximate range of {$23.00} XXXX. However, the alleged foreclosure sale referenced in the communications involved bids reportedly in the approximate range of approximately {$510000.00} to {$570000.00}, representing only a fraction of the propertys estimated value. 

This raises serious concerns regarding the substantial loss of equity associated with the foreclosure process and intensifies the financial harm connected to the disputed foreclosure activity. 

From my perspective, nearly every party connected to this foreclosure process appears positioned to financially benefit from the foreclosure itself including parties connected to servicing, foreclosure administration, legal enforcement, investment acquisition, resale activity, and real estate commissions while I, the homeowner affected by the foreclosure, continue experiencing financial harm, emotional distress, uncertainty, and ongoing displacement pressure. 

XXXX. Pressure Tactics and Emotional Distress The XX/XX/year> communications referenced eviction, urgency, possession demands, and time is of the essence language while encouraging us to leave voluntarily. 

Receiving these communications while disputes remain unresolved created substantial emotional distress and pressure. The communications appeared designed to normalize and accelerate surrender of possession before critical foreclosure-related concerns had been properly addressed. 

XXXX. Concerns Regarding Reliance on Unverified or Disputed Foreclosure Status The letters repeatedly referenced alleged sale completion and ownership transfer, yet significant questions remain concerning the foreclosure process and related representations. 

The continued assertion of ownership rights, possession rights, and transition demands while disputes remain unresolved raises serious concerns regarding : - due diligence, - reliance on potentially disputed foreclosure representations, - and whether parties involved sufficiently verified the legitimacy and finality of the foreclosure process before attempting to obtain possession-related cooperation.

Given that this matter has required multiple CFPB complaints to reach even partial resolution, I can not in good faith accept American Expresss assertion that it has accurately validated the merchant participation status of my transactions. That determination was made internally, on the basis of records American Express has not disclosed, through a process I have had no opportunity to observe or challenge. The history of this dispute does not support extending deference to American Expresss unilateral conclusions. 
American Expresss obligation to investigate billing error claims is not satisfied by a bare assertion that internal records support denial. Under Regulation Z, 12 C.F.R. 1026.13, a card issuer must conduct a reasonable investigation of a disputed billing error and provide the cardholder with a written explanation of its findings, including the basis for its determination. Where, as here, the denial rests entirely on internal participation records, a reasonable investigation requires that those records be disclosed so the cardholder can meaningfully evaluate and, if warranted, rebut the issuers conclusion. Additionally, the Consumer Financial Protection Act prohibits unfair and deceptive acts or practices, 12 U.S.C. 5531 and 5536, and American Expresss practice of denying promotional credits based on undisclosed internal records while operating a broken and now-defunct verification tool is precisely the kind of conduct those provisions are designed to address.

The branch manager also stated, in substance, that as long as she has been working for Chase, no one has ever complained about the foreign currency exchange disclosures. It suggests that Chase branch management and staff may not be properly trained on Chases disclosure obligations or may not understand the compliance risks involved when customers are told there are no fees while Chase may still earn compensation through an embedded spread, commission, vendor payment, or exchange-rate adjustment.

The absence of prior customer complaints does not mean the disclosure was adequate or legally compliant. It may instead indicate that customers were not aware of the embedded cost or did not understand that the exchange rate included compensation to Chase or its vendors. This is precisely why clear, upfront disclosure is necessary. 

I believe Chases conduct was unfair and deceptive. Chases representative told me there were no fees, but Chases receipt indicates that Chase may receive compensation through spreads, vendor payments, and/or commissions. Whether Chase labels the cost as a fee, spread, commission, vendor markup, or exchange-rate adjustment, the practical result was the same : Chase used a materially worse exchange rate and did not clearly disclose the embedded cost before debiting my checking account.

This conduct appears to implicate federal consumer financial protection laws and regulations, including the following : Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices ( UDAAP ). The CFPB states that under the Dodd-Frank Act, it is unlawful for providers of consumer financial products or services to engage in unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices. Chases statement that there were no fees, combined with an undisclosed embedded exchange-rate cost approaching 10 %, raises deceptive and unfair-practice concerns. Its deceptive because Chase did not properly disclose the fees, and tow representative stated there are no fees. Regulation E / Electronic Fund Transfer Act. Because the funds were debited directly from my Chase checking account, this also raises transaction-disclosure and error-resolution concerns. Regulation E applies to electronic fund transfers that authorize a financial institution to debit or credit a consumers account. Chase should explain whether this checking-account debit was treated as an electronic fund transfer and, if so, what disclosures and error-resolution rights applied. 

Truth in Savings Act / Regulation DD. Regulation DD applies to deposit accounts, including checking accounts, and requires disclosures concerning account terms and fee schedules. Regulation DD also provides that a depository institution must provide account disclosures before an account is opened or before a service is provided, whichever is earlier, when a fee required to be disclosed is assessed. Because this currency exchange was funded from my checking account and may have involved account-based pricing, commission waivers, or foreign exchange service charges, Chase should identify the checking-account terms, fee schedule, foreign currency exchange disclosures, commission schedule, waiver terms, and any preferred-pricing provisions that applied.

Because Chase failed to clearly disclose the true cost of the currency exchange, refused to unwind the transaction at the original rate, and instead offered a buy-back rate that would have caused an additional loss, I have lost confidence in Chases handling of my deposit-account services. A dedicated letter, email, secure message, or clearly labeled notice would have appropriately alerted customers to review and respond to the changes. 
Instead, the information was embedded in fine print within a routine monthly statement. Customers primarily use account statements to review balances and transactions, not to search for important contractual changes hidden within the document. Had the change been communicated clearly and prominently, I would have immediately taken action to avoid these fees. 
This communication method feels misleading and predatory because it appears designed in a way that many customers could easily overlook. When fee related changes are quietly placed in statement fine print instead of being communicated through a direct and obvious notification, it creates the impression that the bank benefits financially when customers miss the information. Across a large customer base, this type of communication practice could generate substantial fee revenue from customers who were not meaningfully aware of the changes. 
I had been a Wells Fargo customer for approximately XXXX years and intended to continue banking with them. Because the order had not been fulfilled, I opened multiple disputes with Affirm and repeatedly submitted evidence documenting that the merchant had not shipped the items as claimed. This included screenshots, tracking records, and shipment status information showing no carrier movement or possession of the package during relevant periods. 

During this process, the merchant represented that all items had been shipped. However, only two items were initially delivered ( on XX/XX/XXXX, 6 weeks after order was placed ). The merchant later represented that the remaining items had also been shipped, but again, only one additional item was delivered ( on XX/XX/XXXX ). The final remaining item ( of highest value ) was not delivered until a third shipment was sent in XX/XX/year>, approximately two months after the original order date. Throughout this process, I continued providing Affirm with updated documentation demonstrating that the order had not been fulfilled as represented by the merchant. Despite these inconsistencies and incomplete deliveries, Affirm repeatedly resolved the disputes in favor of the merchant. 

Each time Affirm closed a dispute, I reopened it immediately and continued submitting supporting evidence because the order still had not been fully delivered. 

Once the final item was received, I paid the remaining balance owed to Affirm in two payments. However, despite the account being actively and repeatedly disputed during the prolonged non-fulfillment period, Affirm reported late payments to the credit bureaus. 

I believe Affirm failed to conduct a reasonable investigation into the dispute and improperly furnished derogatory credit information despite extensive notice that : * the transaction was actively disputed, * the merchants fulfillment representations were inconsistent with actual deliveries, * and the order remained only partially fulfilled for an extended period of time.

3. A written explanation of the investigation process used by Affirm to repeatedly deny the disputes despite inconsistent shipment and fulfillment records.

The core issue is not that I ultimately refused payment. I paid the balance once the order was finally fulfilled. The issue is that Affirm reported derogatory information during a prolonged and actively disputed non-fulfillment period despite repeated evidence that the merchant had not fulfilled the order as represented. 

I have retained documentation supporting my position, including dispute records, tracking screenshots, correspondence, shipment records, and payment records.

Issue: Applying for a mortgage or refinancing an existing mortgage
Consumer complaint narrative:
I

am submitting a formal complaint regarding a mortgage lending experience that involved significant communication failures, lack of transparency, and unprofessional handling of our loan process. My partner and I chose to work with this lender based on a previously positive experience, during which we had also referred multiple clients due to the professionalism demonstrated at that time. Unfortunately, this recent transaction fell far below those standards. From the outset, the process was disorganized and lacked clear communication. We were repeatedly asked to submit the same documentationincluding W-2s, pay stubs, and employment explanationsmultiple times, despite having already provided them. This raised concerns regarding proper file review and attention to detail. 

There was also ongoing confusion regarding otherwise straightforward employment information. Despite submitting thorough documentation, including employer verification, we were repeatedly asked for clarification on matters that had already been clearly addressed. In some instances, incorrect assumptions were made about employment history, resulting in unnecessary and irrelevant document requests.

Communication throughout the process was inconsistent and often delayed. On XX/XX/XXXX, we were informed that the loan was in underwriting and that we should expect an update by the following day or Friday. That update was not provided. 

We followed up again on XX/XX/XXXX via email, referencing this commitment and requesting a status update. This email went unanswered.

Additionally, after a subsequent phone conversation, we were told that we would receive an answer within one day. That commitment was not fulfilled at all. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, a request was made for my partner pay stubs again, despite having already provided this documentation previously. This request was made without any explanation or context, and no follow-up communication was provided afterward. Beyond this isolated request, there was no meaningful communication, update, or clarification for approximately three weeks.

This pattern of requesting duplicate documentation without explanation, combined with a lack of follow-up or status updates, contributed to significant confusion and uncertainty regarding the handling of our application.

Throughout this time, closing timelines were repeatedly adjusted without clear explanation, and we were never provided with a definitive approval or denial. 

Additionally, requested documents would appear and then be removed from the system without explanation, creating further confusion and inefficiency.

Most concerning, a substantial change to our loan amount was made without any prior discussion or notification. We only became aware of this change by independently checking the system. A change of this magnitude, which directly impacts financial outcomes, should have been clearly communicated and explained in advance.

We also note that an additional hard credit inquiry was performed during this period of non-communication, without any accompanying explanation or discussion. This is concerning given the absence of ongoing updates or engagement regarding our application.

Due to the lack of communication and inability to move forward, we ultimately sought another lender. With a different lender, we received clear communication and obtained closing approval within 23 weeks. This demonstrates that the delays experienced were not due to our qualifications, but rather deficiencies in communication and process management.

We also paid approximately {$300.00} in application fees and {$670.00} for an appraisal while proceeding in good faith. Given the lack of communication, organization, and overall service, we do not believe the level of service provided justifies retention of the application fee.

We would also like to note that, while we are younger borrowers we entered into this transaction responsibly and in good faith. We expect to be treated with the same level of professionalism, transparency, and respect as any other clients. Regardless of whether the loan was ultimately
viable, clear and honest communication should have been provided.

Instead, we were left without answers and without follow-up, creating the impression that we were not being given the same level of attention or respect that other clients may receive. This is a significant concern.

This experience caused unnecessary stress and uncertainty during a critical financial process. Notably, this occurred during a particularly difficult personal time for our family, which was the death of my spouse sister, which made the absence of communication even more concerning.

We are requesting that this matter be reviewed for professional conduct, particularly regarding failure to communicate, lack of transparency, and mismanagement of a consumer loan application after fees were collected.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

XX/XX/year> Consumer Financial Protection Bureau XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Re : Complaint Against SoLo Funds Undisclosed Lender Fees, Structurally Coercive Fee Model, Deceptive Practices Company : SoLo Funds ( solofunds.com ) Account Type : Lender Account To Whom It May Concern, I am submitting this complaint against SoLo Funds, a peer-to-peer lending platform operating at solofunds.com. I have been an active lender on the platform since XXXX XXXX  and have experienced a pattern of undisclosed fees, misleading disclosures, and what I believe to be a structurally deceptive fee model that disproportionately penalizes lenders while offering borrowers no equivalent accountability.

ISSUE 1 : LENDER FEES ARE NOT DISCLOSED IN THE LOAN AGREEMENT SoLo Funds presents lenders with a standard Loan Agreement and Promissory Note at the time each loan is funded. I have reviewed this agreement carefully and can confirm that it contains XXXX disclosure of any fees that may be charged to the lender.

The loan agreement in its entirety identifies the following fee obligations all of which apply exclusively to the borrower : Late Fee ( 15 % of principal or {$5.00}, whichever is greater ) charged to the borrower Transaction Fee ( 2x [ 0.9 % of principal + {$0.00} ] ) charged to the borrower Returned Payment Fee ( {$15.00} ) charged to the borrower There is no mention anywhere in the loan agreement of any fee that could be assessed against the lender under any circumstance. A lender reviewing this document has every reasonable basis to conclude that they are not subject to any platform-imposed fees.

Despite this, SoLo Funds imposes a fee of 12 % to 15 % of the loan principal on lenders when a borrower is late a fee that entirely eliminates, and in some cases exceeds, the tip income the lender expected to earn. This fee was not disclosed in the loan agreement, is not referenced at the point of loan funding, and was not communicated to me until after it had been applied to my account. 
This constitutes a material omission in financial disclosure and a deceptive practice under the Consumer Financial Protection Act 's prohibition on Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices ( UDAAP ).

ISSUE 2 : THE FEE STRUCTURE IS STRUCTURALLY COERCIVE Even setting aside the lack of disclosure, the mechanics of how this fee is applied reveal a model that is structurally unfair to lenders. Here is how it actually works : The 35-Day Window : The loan agreement grants borrowers a 35-day repayment term from the funding date. During this window, the borrower faces no late fees whatsoever as confirmed by the agreements own terms. The lender, however, has no equivalent grace period. If a borrower repays even one or two days past their agreed repayment date, the lender is immediately assessed the 12 % 15 % fee.

The Asymmetry : The borrower has 35 days before any penalty applies to them.

The lender is penalized the moment the borrowers self-selected due date passes even if the loan is still within the 35-day contractual window.

The borrowers fees ( when they do apply after 35 days ) accrue to the platform, not to the lender. The lender receives no compensation for the borrowers lateness.

The Only Two Choices for Lenders : SoLo Funds has structured a system in which lenders have essentially two options to avoid the late fee : 1. Hope that the borrower pays on exactly the agreed due date a circumstance entirely outside the lenders control ; or 2. Pre-purchase SoLo Lender Protection ( SLP ) at a cost of 5 % to 6 % of the loan principal, paid upfront.

In practical terms, this means that a lender who does not purchase SLP is routinely penalized for borrower behavior they can not control. The only way to avoid the penalty is to pay a protection fee in advance. This is not a voluntary product it is effectively a mandatory cost of doing business on the platform, disguised as optional. This is a textbook example of an abusive practice : SoLo Funds leverages an information asymmetry and structural imbalance to extract additional fees from lenders who reasonably believed they had no exposure to platform-imposed charges.

ISSUE 3 : INCONSISTENT FEE DISCLOSURES FROM CUSTOMER SERVICE Upon contacting SoLo Funds customer service and their automated IQ Chat Bot to understand the fee structure, I received materially inconsistent information : One representative cited the late fee as 15 % ; another cited 12 % The threshold at which Lender Protection is waived was stated as the first XXXX loans in XXXX interaction, then corrected to XXXX loans in another This inconsistency in the disclosure of material financial terms further demonstrates that SoLo Funds does not have clear, accurate, or accessible fee disclosures and that the companys own representatives can not reliably explain the fee model to lenders.

ISSUE 4 : PATTERN OF NON-RESPONSIVE CUSTOMER SERVICE I have contacted SoLo Funds customer service on multiple occasions regarding these issues. In each instance, I received generic, templated responses that failed to engage with the specific questions I raised. No written explanation of the lender fee structure has been provided. No refund or credit has been offered. No representative has been able to provide documentation of where, in any agreement I signed, the lender fee is disclosed.

FINANCIAL HARM As a direct result of these undisclosed fees, I have sustained measurable financial losses. During my current lending period, XXXX of XXXX active loans are late. The 12 % has been applied to those loans; eliminated all tip income I expected to earn and resulted in a net loss on lending activity I undertook in good faith, based on the terms disclosed to me at the time of funding.

Midland Credit Management , Inc. ( " Midland Credit '' ) has attempted to collect from me on four consumer accounts ( MCM # XXXX, # XXXX, # XXXX, and # XXXX ) while sending me written correspondence that does not comply with the licensing-disclosure requirements imposed on collection agencies in North Carolina , the State where I reside and where the collection activity is directed. Midland Credit has now confirmed this non-compliance in writing to a federal regulator and continues to furnish information about these accounts to the three major consumer reporting agencies. 
I have previously raised related issues through CFPB Case # XXXX and NC DOJ XXXX XXXX. XXXX. Midland Credits response letters of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  do not address the federal violations described below. I am filing this complaint to place those federal violations directly before the Bureau. 
Issue 1 Federal violations arising from collection correspondence that omits required state licensing disclosure ( 15 U.S.C. 1692e ( 5 ), 1692e ( 10 ), and 1692f ) North Carolina law requires that " [ a ] ll collection agencies licensed under this statute doing business of a collection agency in this State, shall in all correspondence with debtors use stationery or forms which contain the permit number and the true name and address of such collection agency. '' XXXX XXXX XXXX. XXXX. The North Carolina Department of Insurance ( " NCDOI '' ) administers this Article and issues the collection-agency permits to which XXXX refers. 
Midland Credits XXXX XXXX XXXX letter ( to NC DOJ regarding File No. XXXX ) and XXXX XXXX XXXX letter ( to the CFPB regarding Case # XXXX ) both expressly state, " This communication is from a debt collector. '' Both letters were sent to me as the consumer. Neither letter, from Midland Credit, contains a North Carolina collection agency permit number on the stationery or anywhere in the body of the correspondence. 
When I raised this issue in my prior CFPB complaint, Midland Credits XXXX XXXX XXXX response declined to provide the permit number. It stated only that the company is " licensed and/or bonded in every state which requires such licensing and/or bonding for collection companies '' and instructed me to " contact your local state office for more information regarding licensing requirements. '' Midland Credit has now affirmatively, in writing, both ( a ) confirmed that its correspondence with me does not contain the disclosure required by XXXX, and ( b ) declined to bring the correspondence into compliance. 
I am not asking the Bureau to enforce N.C. Gen. Stat. XXXX directly. I am identifying federal violations that arise from this conduct : Violation of 15 U.S.C. 1692e and 1692e ( 10 ) false representation or deceptive means. 
By sending collection correspondence to me that holds itself out as the work of a duly licensed collection agency while omitting the statutorily required permit number, Midland Credit uses deceptive means to create the appearance of regulatory legitimacy that the correspondence itself, on its face, does not establish. Courts have recognized that a debt collectors failure to comply with state licensing-related disclosure requirements, where the collector nonetheless communicates with the consumer as a licensed entity, can constitute a 1692e violation. The Bureaus own Regulation F preamble and supervisory guidance treat state licensing compliance as a foundational element of lawful debt collection practice. 
Violation of 15 U.S.C. 1692e ( 5 ) threats to take action that can not legally be taken. 
Midland Credits XXXX XXXX XXXX letter affirmatively states that " account nos. XXXX and XXXX had been determined to be eligible for legal efforts '' and that " non-payment on the accounts may result in the accounts being forwarded to a law firm in [ my ] area to review for possible legal efforts to collect the balance. '' A debt collector that is operating in non-compliance with state licensing-disclosure requirements is not in a position to make such representations, and using the threat of legal action while simultaneously refusing to provide the state-required licensing disclosure violates 1692e ( 5 ).

Violation of 15 U.S.C. 1692f unfair or unconscionable means. 
Continuing to attempt to collect a debt, and continuing to furnish information about that debt to consumer reporting agencies, while operating in admitted non-compliance with the states correspondence-disclosure requirements, is an unfair means of collection within the meaning of 1692f. The consumer is denied the ability to verify, on the face of the correspondence, that the entity demanding payment is operating within the regulatory framework that authorizes it to do so.

Issue 2 Additional context : third-party disclosure through email subject lines ( 15 U.S.C. 1692c ( b ) ) As additional context showing a pattern of non-compliance, Midland Credit has previously sent me email collection communications with subject lines that disclose or expressly reference the existence of the debt, including " XXXX, youve got some unfinished business, '' " XXXX, Please Address Your Financial Commitment, '' " XXXX, Accept Your Low Payment Option, '' and similar formulations. Midland Credits response to this issue in my prior CFPB complaint stated only that the subject lines were " reviewed and approved '' by its legal team and that the company " does not have control over an individual users settings on devices, applications, or email service providers. '' That response did not address the substance of the 1692c ( b ) concern. I have retained dated copies and screenshots of these communications and will produce them on request. I raise this here primarily as evidence of a broader pattern of treating consumer-facing compliance obligations as discretionary. 
What Midland Credits prior responses do not establish They do not provide a North Carolina collection agency permit number on the correspondence. 
They do not deny that the correspondence omits the permit number. 
They affirmatively decline to bring future correspondence into compliance, instead instructing me to contact a state office. 
They do not substantively address the 1692c ( b ) subject-line concern.

They do not provide documentation of the source of, or consent associated with, the email address used to contact me, as called for under the email procedures of 12 C.F.R. 1006.6 ( d ) ( 4 ).

Parallel filings I have filed a separate complaint with the NC Department of Insurance regarding the XXXX issue and a written dispute and notice-of-violation letter directly with Midland Credit by certified mail XXXX This CFPB complaint addresses the federal-law violations arising from the same underlying conduct. 
Fair Resolution ( " What would be a fair resolution? '' field ) I am requesting that Midland Credit Management , Inc. : 1. Delete the tradelines for MCM accounts # XXXX, # XXXX, # XXXX, and # XXXX from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, as a remedy for the federal violations described above, and confirm deletion in writing. A debt collector that has communicated with me in non-compliance with the state licensing-disclosure law, and has affirmatively declined to come into compliance after notice, should not be furnishing information about the collection effort to consumer reporting agencies. 
2. Identify, on the response itself, Midland Credits North Carolina collection agency permit number, and confirm in writing that all future correspondence with North Carolina debtors will include the permit number as required by XXXX. 
3. Provide a substantive written response to the 1692e, 1692e ( 5 ), 1692e ( 10 ), and 1692f issues identified above not a reference back to prior correspondence.

4. Provide documentation showing the source from which Midland Credit obtained the email address used to contact me, and the consent ( or original creditors permissible transfer of consent under 12 C.F.R. 1006.6 ( d ) ( 4 ) ) authorizing electronic communications regarding these accounts.

Attached as supporting documentation is a mini-statement from my financial institution, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX, reflecting the underlying account activity associated with these transactions.

However, substantially similar payments involving : approximately {$4000.00} to the XXXX XXXX XXXX associated with XXXX XXXX ; and approximately {$5000.00} to Citibank were subjected to extended payment holds despite the funds already having been withdrawn from my bank account. 
In both cases : the ACH payments were successfully initiated, the funds were removed from my checking account, the payments originated from a long-established verified bank account, and there were no fraud alerts reported by my financial institution. 

I contacted my bank directly and was informed that no fraud flags or suspicious activity indicators existed on my account in connection with these transactions. 
I subsequently contacted both credit-card issuers multiple times and escalated the matter to supervisory personnel. During those conversations, I was informed that the transactions had been automatically flagged because of the payment amounts involved and that the restrictions were system generated.

This raises significant concerns regarding : the transparency of these automated payment-hold systems, the absence of meaningful manual review, and the possibility that legitimate consumer payments are being broadly restricted through opaque algorithmic processes despite confirmed withdrawal and settlement of funds.

Under the FCRA, a collection is a derivative record. Because there is no primary " anchor '' tradeline, there is no independent way to verify the Date of First Delinquency ( DOFD ). Substantial Financial Harm and Mortgage Impact This unverified and erroneous reporting is causing significant financial harm by interfering with a pending mortgage transaction. Before XXXX completed the loss mitigation evaluation, my loan was transferred to Carrington Mortgage Services , LLC . The pending modification review had not been completed by XXXX before transfer. Under 12 C.F.R. 1024.41 ( k ), Carrington was required as the transferee servicer to honor the complete loss mitigation application that XXXX received on XX/XX/XXXX, and to continue the evaluation rather than restart or cancel it.

Carrington has since taken the following actions, each of which I believe violates federal mortgage servicing law and FHA loss mitigation requirements : ( 1 ) Carrington demanded lump-sum repayment of the entire forborne amount and threatened foreclosure. FHA loss mitigation guidance under HUD Handbook 4000.1 does not permit servicers to require lump-sum repayment of forborne amounts as a precondition for bringing an FHA-insured loan current. Multiple FHA loss mitigation options including the COVID-19 Recovery Modification, FHA-HAMP, Standalone Partial Claim, and Recovery Standalone Partial Claim must be evaluated before foreclosure can proceed.

( 2 ) Carrington cancelled my complete loss mitigation application without providing any written notice or written decision. During a phone call, Carrington informed me that my application had been cancelled because they had attempted to call me for a " second attestation '' and I did not answer. I never received any written request from Carrington for additional documentation, any written request for an attestation, or any written notice of cancellation. This violates 12 C.F.R. 1024.41 ( c ), which requires a written decision stating the specific reason for any denial of a complete loss mitigation application. It also violates 12 C.F.R. 1024.41 ( b ) ( 2 ) ( i ) ( B ), which requires the servicer to provide written notice specifying what additional information is needed and a reasonable deadline to provide it. A missed phone call is not a permitted basis for cancellation under Regulation X.

( 3 ) On XX/XX/XXXX, Carrington issued a Maryland Notice of Intent to Foreclose under Maryland Real Property Article 7-105.1 ( c ). The notice lists my Date of Default as XX/XX/XXXX a date that falls within my active XXXX FHA Special Forbearance Plan, during which my contractual monthly payment was {$0.00}. The notice claims my loan is 269 days past due and demands {$21000.00} to cure. Carrington also elected not to offer prefile mediation. Under the Notice of Intent to Foreclose, a foreclosure action ( Order to Docket ) may be filed in Circuit Court as early as XX/XX/XXXX. 
( 4 ) Carrington has not provided me with a single point of contact for my loss mitigation file, in violation of 12 C.F.R. 1024.40.

( 5 ) Carrington has engaged in conduct consistent with prohibited " dual tracking '' under 12 C.F.R. 1024.41 ( f ) and ( g ) by issuing a Notice of Intent to Foreclose while a complete loss mitigation application received by the prior servicer on XX/XX/XXXX should have remained pending under federal law.

The cumulative effect of Carrington 's actions is that an improperly calculated default has been used to initiate Maryland foreclosure proceedings against my primary residence, despite the existence of written documentation from the prior servicer establishing both ( a ) an active forbearance plan with {$0.00} contractually due during the disputed default period, and ( b ) a complete loss mitigation application that was pending evaluation at the time of servicing transfer.

I have attached the following supporting documentation : XXXX FHA Special Forbearance Plan Approval dated XX/XX/XXXX ; XXXX Forbearance Plan Completion Notice dated XX/XX/XXXX ; XXXX Post-Forbearance Acknowledgment of Complete Application dated XX/XX/XXXX ; and Carrington Notice of Intent to Foreclose dated XX/XX/XXXX. 
I am simultaneously filing a complaint with the Maryland Commissioner of Financial Regulation and am submitting a Mortgage Assistance Application and formal cover letter directly to Carrington requesting reinstatement of my loss mitigation evaluation as of XX/XX/XXXX. 
Given that Carrington may file an Order to Docket in Circuit Court as early as XX/XX/XXXX, I respectfully request expedited review of this complaint. 

A few things this narrative does deliberately It opens with XXXXXXXX XXXX written record, not your hardship. Reviewers triage hundreds of complaints. The strongest hook isn't " I'm in trouble '' it's " the prior servicer 's written documents contradict the current servicer 's actions. '' That framing makes the violation pattern obvious from the first paragraph. 
It quotes XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXXXX/XX/XXXX letter directly. That single sentence " We have sufficient information to evaluate you for a loan modification, and we consider your application complete as of XX/XX/XXXX '' is the most powerful sentence in your entire file. Burying it would be a mistake. Quoting it ensures the reviewer reads it.

It numbers the violations. Reviewers love enumerated lists because they can map each numbered item to a specific regulatory citation and require Carrington to respond to each one. A flowing narrative is easier to wave away ; a numbered list is not.

It puts the math dispute front and center. The XX/XX/XXXX default date during a documented forbearance period is the single most exploitable factual error in Carrington 's case. It appears twice once in item ( 3 ) and once in the closing paragraph to ensure no reviewer misses it.

It closes with the urgency hook. The XX/XX/XXXX potential filing date is the single most important fact for triage prioritization. Putting it in the final sentence guarantees the reviewer sees it when deciding queue priority.

No personal info, per the form 's instruction. No name, no address, no loan numbers, no SSN. The CFPB form collects all of that separately. This field is pure narrative.

Issue: Problem with a company's investigation into an existing problem
Consumer complaint narrative:
To Whom It May Concern, I am filing this complaint against Upstart XXXX XXXX XXXX regarding inaccurate, incomplete, and misleading credit reporting on my loan account XXXX. 

Upstart reported my account as 30 days late for the XX/XX/year> payment period. However, I had automatic payments set up and acted in good faith to make my payments. The issue was not caused by intentional nonpayment or refusal to pay. It appears to have involved payment processing, ACH/banking restrictions, and unclear or conflicting payment information. 

The main concern is that Upstarts own system sent me payment confirmations that reasonably led me to believe my payments were processed. On XX/XX/year>, Upstart emailed me stating that my automatic payment of {$60.00} had been processed from my XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX checking account ending in XXXX. On XX/XX/year>, Upstart sent another confirmation stating that a payment of {$63.00} had been applied to my loan and that my card ending in XXXX had been debited. 

Despite these confirmations, Upstart later claimed that the XX/XX/XXXX, XX/XX/XXXX, and XX/XX/XXXX payments were returned as unsuccessful and reported the account as XXXX as of XX/XX/year>. This creates a direct conflict between Upstarts payment confirmation emails and the negative credit reporting. 

I disputed the reporting directly with Upstart and explained that the issue was caused by a payment/banking problem, not neglect or inability to pay. I also explained that the account had been brought current and requested removal of the 30-day late reporting. Upstart refused to remove the late reporting, stating that no internal error was found.

I then requested a final escalation and asked Upstart to reconcile its internal records, including the system-generated payment confirmations, returned payment codes, and credit reporting. I specifically requested a manual review because Upstarts own payment confirmations conflicted with its decision to report the account late. Instead of providing a full reconciliation, Upstart stated that the matter was resolved and that no further communication would be provided. 

I believe this raises concerns under the Fair Credit Reporting Act and the California Consumer Credit Reporting Agencies Act, including California Civil Code 1785.25.

Under California Civil Code 1785.25 ( a ), a furnisher should not report information to a consumer credit reporting agency if it knows or should know the information is incomplete or inaccurate. In this case, Upstart had payment confirmations generated by its own system, yet still reported the account as 30 days late without fully reconciling the conflicting information.

Under California Civil Code 1785.25 ( b ), if a furnisher determines that information previously reported is incomplete or inaccurate, it must promptly correct or update that information with the credit reporting agencies. I provided Upstart with notice of the conflicting payment confirmations, but Upstart refused to correct or meaningfully review the reporting.

Under California Civil Code 1785.25 ( c ), when the accuracy or completeness of reported information remains disputed by the consumer, the furnisher should not continue reporting the information without noting that it is disputed. I have repeatedly disputed this reporting and request confirmation that any continued reporting includes a consumer dispute notation.

Dear Capital Management Services , LP, I am writing to formally request both verification and validation of the alleged debt you claim I owe, in accordance with my rights under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ( FDCPA ), Section 809 ( b ). Verification and validation are distinct legal concepts, and I demand that you provide both.

Verification is the process of confirming whether I actually owe the debt, as referenced in Chaudhry v. Gallerizzo, 174 F.3d 394 ( 4th Cir. 1999 ). According to Blacks Law Dictionary, verification is defined as an averment that the party pleading is ready to establish the truth of what he has set forth. The examination of a writing for the purpose of ascertaining its truth ; or a certificate or affidavit that it is true. In McDonald v. Rosengarten, 134 Ill. 126, 25 N.E. ( 1890 ), the court explained that verification involves the " confirmation of the correctness, truth, or authenticity of a pleading, account, or other paper, by an affidavit, oath, or deposition. '' Other courts, such as in Summerfield v. Phoenix Assur. Co. ( C. C. ) 65 Fed. 296 ( 1922 ) and Patterson v. Brooklyn, 6 App. Div. 127, 40 N.Y. Supp. 581 ( 1898 ), have reiterated this legal principle. 

Therefore, I request the following : Proof that I am legally responsible for the debt in question. A verified statement of the original creditor and the contract or agreement that created the debt.

Validation is necessary to confirm the legitimacy of this debt before any further action can be taken, as referenced in Spears v. Brennan, 745 N.E. 2d 862 Ind. App. ( 2001 ). Black 's Law Dictionary defines validation as assessing an action to determine it is complete, correct, implemented, and delivering the correct outcome. Oxford defines it as to check or prove the validity or accuracy of something, and Merriam-Webster explains it as to show the existence or truth of, by evidence. 

To this end, I am requesting that you provide : Validation of the debt, including a breakdown of how the amount was calculated, itemizing any interest, fees, or charges added to the original balance.

Documentation proving that your agency is authorized to collect the debt on behalf of the original creditor. Any judgment or legal order obtained against me regarding this debt ( if applicable ). Proof that the debt is not time-barred under the statute of limitations in my state.

Until you provide both verification and validation of the debt, I request that you cease all collection activities, including reporting this alleged debt to any credit reporting agencies, as required by the FDCPA.

Please respond with the requested information within 30 days of receipt of this letter. If you can not provide the necessary verification and validation, I expect you to remove any record of this debt and cease all collection efforts.

Thank you for your immediate attention to this matter. I look forward to receiving the proper documentation. 

Sincerely, XXXX XXXX

NOTICE OF RESCISSION DUE TO MISREPRESENTATION AND FRAUD Based on the documents provided, here is an argument for Misrepresentation by Sunlight Financial.

The core of this argument rests on the internal contradictions between Sunlights legal assertions and the actual language of their contracts regarding the nature of the collateral and the security interest.

Argument : Fraudulent Misrepresentation of Security Interest and Loan Characterization 1. Contradictory Definitions of Collateral In Exhibit A, Sunlight Financial explicitly denies that they hold a security interest in the consumers principal dwelling. They state that the loan is " defined and treated as personal property '' and that no " encumbrance has been placed on the residence. '' However, Exhibit C-1 directly contradicts this. The contract language states that Sunlight may make a " fixture filing '' and, crucially, that they may " enforce rights in the Equipment ... under state real estate or mortgage law. '' * The Misrepresentation : Sunlight can not claim the loan is " strictly limited '' to personal property ( to avoid Truth in Lending Act rescission rights ) while simultaneously reserving the right to use " mortgage law '' to enforce their interest. By claiming the interest is not real-estate related, they may be attempting to circumvent consumer protection laws ( like 12 C.F.R. 1026.23 ) that apply when a dwelling is used as collateral.

2. Misleading Characterization of the " Project '' In Exhibit C, the contract describes the transaction as a " home improvement project. '' * Standard industry and legal definitions typically treat " home improvements '' as enhancements to the real property.

By labeling it a " home improvement project '' in the disclosure but later insisting in Exhibit A that it is strictly " personal property '' ( like a refrigerator or a car ), Sunlight and XXXX XXXX XXXX are using shifting definitions to suit their legal needs while keeping the consumer in the dark about the true nature of the lien on their home.

3. Admission via " Corrective '' Action In Exhibit D, Sunlight states they have initiated the termination of the fixture filing ( UCC-3 ) " without taking any position on the legal analysis. '' The Argument : While they frame this as a resolution, it serves as evidence of an Improper Filing. If the filing were legitimate and correctly represented in the original loan agreement, there would be no reason to terminate it in response to a formal complaint.

The fact that they are removing the fixture filing suggests that the original filing was either unauthorized by the loans stated terms or was an attempt to cloud the property title without granting the consumer the legal protections ( like the right of rescission ) that come with real estate-collateralized loans.

4. Failure of Due Diligence A lender or agent is responsible for the accuracy of the disclosures provided to the borrower.

The bank allowed a " Fixture Filing '' to be executed ( which attaches to the real estate records ) while providing disclosures stating that no such interest in the residence existed.

This discrepancy between the recorded public filing and the private loan disclosures constitutes a material misrepresentation that affects the borrower 's ability to refinance or sell their home.

Concealment of Rescission Rights Under Federal Law The contradictory disclosures and shifting legal characterizations appear designed to circumvent protections afforded under the federal Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ), including the borrowers right of rescission under 15 U.S.C. 1635 and Regulation Z, 12 C.F.R. 1026.23.

Where a creditor acquires, claims, or reserves rights associated with a security interest in a consumers principal dwelling, clear and accurate disclosures are required.

The failure to accurately disclose : the existence of the claimed interest, the legal effect of the fixture filing, the use of mortgage-law enforcement rights, and the true nature of the collateral constitutes a material disclosure violation.

I was informed that there had been multiple failed authorization attempts and failed CVV attempts before the transactions were eventually approved. I was also informed by a representative on the phone with my local bank agent that additional suspicious activity involving attempted ACH activity or related account activity occurred after the debit card fraud. Due to these fraud concerns, Bank of America restricted my account to credit only status and opened a replacement account for me.

Pursuant to the Fair Credit Billing Act, as implemented through Regulation Z, card issuers are legally obligated to investigate billing disputes involving goods or services not accepted by the consumer or not delivered as agreed. Specifically, 12 C.F.R. 1026.13 ( a ) provides protections where transactions involve goods or services that are materially deficient, defective, or not delivered in accordance with the merchants representations.

Accordingly, XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX has a legal obligation to conduct a reasonable, comprehensive, and good-faith investigation into these disputed transactions.

The disputed amount substantially exceeds the statutory threshold required under applicable federal law. 

Federal law further requires that, upon receipt of a timely written billing dispute notice, the card issuer must : Acknowledge the dispute within thirty ( 30 ) days ; Conduct a reasonable and thorough investigation into the disputed transactions ; Resolve the dispute within two complete billing cycles, not exceeding ninety ( 90 ) days ; and Credit the consumers account if the investigation confirms that a billing error occurred.
